articles.title: ChargePoint and PistenBully have a charging plan for ski resorts
articles.description: ChargePoint and PistenBully maker Kässbohrer are bringing EV chargers for electric snow groomers and visitors’ EVs to ski resorts.
paragraphs: The next EV to plug in at a ski resort might be the one that groomed your trail. ChargePoint has struck a deal with Kässbohrer, the German company behind PistenBully snow groomers, to bring charging to ski resorts and indoor ski facilities across Europe and North America.

Under the agreement, Kässbohrer will connect its customers with ChargePoint for chargers, software, and support with planning, installation, and day-to-day operations. Resorts can use the same provider for the snow groomers and other vehicles they keep at the maintenance depot, as well as for the EV chargers skiers use while they’re out on the slopes.

Kässbohrer’s first fully electric groomer, the PistenBully 100 E, uses electric motors to move the machine and spin the tiller that smooths the snow. It has a 196 kWh battery and can handle up to three hours of normal grooming on a charge, according to the manufacturer. It can take up to 22 kW on AC or 150 kW on a DC fast charger. It fast charges from zero to 100% in about an hour.

ChargePoint says Kässbohrer accounts for more than half of the snow groomers sold worldwide each year. Resorts can start working with the companies now. Which resorts will install ChargePoint’s chargers first, and how many will go in, are TBC.

Tesla quietly sets up a company at German machine maker EMAG’s HQ
articles.description: Tesla registered a new company at machine-tool maker EMAG's German HQ. Local reports say 220 EMAG workers could join Tesla to work on humanoid robots.
paragraphs: Tesla has registered a new German company whose business address is the headquarters of EMAG, a struggling machine-tool maker that builds production equipment for the gears inside humanoid robots.
Neither company confirmed a deal. But the paper trail is hard to ignore, and it lines up neatly with Tesla’s push to mass-produce Optimus.

The company is called Tesla Machining Technologies Management SE. Germany’s official company register lists it under HRB 315756 at the Munich district court, with €120,000 in share capital and a business address of Austraße 24 in Salach, a small town east of Stuttgart. That’s EMAG’s home base.

It didn’t start out as a Tesla company. The register shows it was first entered on August 26 as “Blitz 26-299 SE,” a shell company. Law firms sell these pre-registered shells so buyers can skip weeks of incorporation paperwork, and Tesla renamed this one earlier this month.

Business Insider Germany, which reported the change based on a notice in the federal gazette, says three people run it: Maximilian Stromberger, Tesla Germany’s 33-year-old head of sales, an American robotics engineer, and the head of HR at Tesla’s Grünheide factory.
The HR chief is the interesting name. You don’t need one to hold a passive stake in a supplier, but you do if you’re about to take on employees.

Local press near Salach has been on this for over a week. On November 23, the Stuttgarter Nachrichten reported that signs of a Tesla entry were piling up and that EMAG had briefed its workforce at a large staff meeting the week before. Business Insider dates that meeting to November 16.

Today, the same paper went further. It reports that around 220 EMAG employees will move to Tesla, that the two companies have been working together for some time, and that the deal is about humanoid robots. The full story is paywalled, and none of it has been confirmed by either company.

EMAG, with roots going back to 1867, makes turning, grinding, and gear-cutting machines, mostly for car parts like transmissions and drivetrains. The auto slowdown hit it hard. A year ago, EMAG said it would cut 455 jobs in Germany, roughly 300 of them in Salach, which is about a third of its domestic staff. It lost €42 million on €496 million of revenue in 2024, per Business Insider. It has been talking to potential investors ever since.
But EMAG has also been chasing a new market. Its website has an entire section on manufacturing humanoid robot actuator parts: flexsplines, wave generators, and planetary gears.
articles.lede: Tesla registered a new company at machine-tool maker EMAG's German HQ. Local reports say 220 EMAG workers could join Tesla to work on humanoid robots.

Toyota is about to unveil its first extended-range EV, and it looks like the Highlander
articles.description: Toyota is set to reveal its first extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) on November 27, and from the first look, it...
paragraphs: Toyota is set to reveal its first extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) on November 27, and from the first look, it could be based on its flagship Highlander SUV.
The EREV is Toyota’s fifth “electrified” vehicle, a term that now spans pure electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), hybrids (HEVs), and fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEVs).
Unlike fully electric vehicles, an EREV also uses a gas engine that serves as a generator to recharge the battery when it gets low, thereby extending the driving range.

EREVs use a smaller battery than a pure electric vehicle, while the engine is typically smaller than a PHEV. While they are quieter and often cheaper than a plug-in, EREVs are also less efficient than a pure EV.
A Nikkei report in September claimed that Toyota was preparing to begin production of its first EREV in China in Spring 2027.
It appears the rumors are true. Toyota’s joint venture in China, GAC Toyota, posted a preview on its Weibo account with the caption #Toyota doesn’t rush but range-extended.

Toyota didn’t confirm the name, but all signs point to it being the Highlander EREV. The blurry preview looks like the Highlander, and when translated into English, a part of the text below it reads “Cash in on the classics. Global flagship SUV. Not a quick fix, but a range extender.”
GAC Toyota will reveal the new EREV at the Guangzhou Motor Show on November 27. Check back for the full details.
According to the Nikkei report, Toyota aims to produce 200,000 EREVs in 2027. In 2028, it expects production to double to around 400,000 units.
While Toyota likely won’t bring the extended-range EV to the US, it is set to launch the fully electric version of its three-row Highlander in early 2027 (shown above on the left).
articles.lede: Toyota is set to reveal its first extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) on November 27, and from the first look, it could be based on its flagship Highlander SUV.

articles.title: Hyundai IONIQ 3 spotted on US roads: Is the affordable EV coming to the US? [update]
articles.description: Hyundai’s new IONIQ 3 checks all the boxes as an affordable EV: it offers over 300 miles of range, a practical...
paragraphs: Hyundai’s new IONIQ 3 checks all the boxes as an affordable EV: it offers over 300 miles of range, a practical interior, and Hyundai’s new Pleos infotainment system. So, will Hyundai bring it to the US?
The Hyundai IONIQ 3 is now on sale across Europe and the UK as a smaller sibling to the IONIQ 5, positioned between the Inster EV and Hyundai Kona Electric.

Although it’s part of the IONIQ sub-brand, the IONIQ 3 features a new “Aero Hatch” design. The new look “reimagines the compact EV silhouette,” Hyundai said, designed to optimize efficiency and interior space.
The response so far has been “extraordinary,” Ashley Andrew, president of Hyundai Motor UK, said after launching the IONIQ 3 last month.

According to Andrew, the compact EV received “more customers registering their interest before launch than any new Hyundai we’ve introduced in the UK,” and that’s including gas-powered and electric vehicles.
The first reviews of the IONIQ 3 have been overwhelmingly positive, highlighting its efficiency, practical interior, and affordable price tag.

Update 11/25/2026: A Hyundai spokesperson told Electrek that “it’s likely that the IONIQ 3 that was apparently spotted in the US recently was the same unit that was brought in for World Car of the Year’s annual test days” held in Pasadena, California.
It looks like the IONIQ 3 will be another affordable, practical EV the US will miss out on.
The update from Hyundai comes after the IONIQ 3 was recently captured driving on public US roads, raising speculation, or perhaps hope, that it will come to the States after all.
The model spotted in the images from KindelAuto is the IONIQ 3 N Line, a sportier, higher-priced trim.
articles.lede: Hyundai’s new IONIQ 3 checks all the boxes as an affordable EV: it offers over 300 miles of range, a practical interior, and Hyundai’s new Pleos infotainment system. So, will Hyundai bring it to the US?

Google’s grid deal in Ohio tests a faster path to data center power
articles.description: Google plans to spend $10.8 million on advanced transmission technology, and hopes other tech giants will adopt its model.
paragraphs: Google and Ohio Power plan to test a new way for the hyperscaler to pay for advanced transmission upgrades, potentially unlocking faster access to power and shielding other customers from the costs.

Those advanced conductors are expected to unlock 700 MW of additional headroom on the grid compared to a standard rebuild by 2031. That boost depends on a separate transmission project underway by Ohio Power and other partners coming online by 2031. Some 300-miles of new lines would bring more power into central Ohio, and advanced conductors can carry between 40% to 70% more electricity than conventional wires. This’ll allow Ohio Power to squeeze more power out of an existing corridor.

The first-of-its-kind approach comes as hyperscalers are under pressure to pay for their own energy costs and more, especially after so many candidates who campaigned on the issue won their races in the midterms.

“We want to demonstrate that this kind of investment can work, not just for our data center pipeline but to enable a significant amount of more headroom for other customers in a utility’s service territory,” Ellen Zuckerman, Google’s head of energy market development for North and South America, told Latitude Media. “This is a path others can hopefully follow to unlock capacity that exists on the grid today if we deploy more innovative technologies.”

Higher capacity conductors are among a suite of advanced transmission technologies that utilities could deploy on the grid. ATTs can be faster and cheaper than building new lines, saving ratepayers money over the long term and helping unlock the speed-to-power data center developers demand.

Advanced conductors can cost 33% to 75% less than a new transmission line while unlocking double the capacity, according to separate studies by the Department of Energy, and researchers at GridLab and UC Berkeley. But adoption by incumbent utilities has been slow, in part because their profit model overseen by state regulators rewards spending over efficiency, and ATTs can lack clear cost-recovery pathways.

Zuckerman said there are a lot of barriers to getting advanced conductors on the grid, including the utility profit model and installers’ unfamiliarity with the technology. But Google and AEP — the parent of Ohio Power — have a track record of innovation, she added, citing the clean transition tariff launched in 2024. The tariff is aimed at allowing Google to pay a higher rate for power to fund emerging generation technologies, such as advanced geothermal or long-duration energy storage.

Google’s investment in advanced reconductors is an extension of that work, Zuckerman said. “You can think of this as expanding the clean transition tariff from generation to also incorporating the transmission system.”

Ohio in 2025 also enacted a law directing state regulators to map out how data centers and other large load customers can partner with utilities to deploy ATTs. That law is part of a broader push by state and federal policymakers to accelerate adoption.
articles.lede: Google plans to spend $10.8 million on advanced transmission technology, and hopes other tech giants will adopt its model.

articles.title: The Suzuki Ignis is back, and this time it will be a low-cost EV sold globally [Images]
articles.description: Suzuki offered a first look at the all-new Ignis, its first compact EV designed specifically for global markets. Suzuki revives...
paragraphs: The first-generation Ignis went on sale back in 2000 as a three- and five-door hatchback, and in 2016, Suzuki reintroduced it as a compact crossover.
After discontinuing the gas-powered version just last year, Suzuki is now bringing the Ignis back. This time, as a fully electric compact EV.
Suzuki revealed the all-new Ignis EV on Wednesday, deeming it the brand’s “first compact EV for global markets.”
The electric city car is based on the original Ignis and clearly draws inspiration from the e Sky, Suzuki’s first kei EV that debuted last month in Japan.

Unlike the e Sky, the new Ignis EV is designed for global markets, including Europe. Suzuki said the Ignis was developed under the concept of “Easy to Switch,” which, as you can guess, means it’s designed to make it easy for drivers to switch from a gas-powered car to electric.
To ensure it can handle urban areas and winding roads in Europe and other regions, Suzuki put the electric city car through “extensive testing” on public roads.
Suzuki fine-tuned the chassis and power delivery specifically for the different road conditions and needs of drivers in major global markets.
The global Ignis EV is also slightly larger than the e Sky, measuring 3,570 mm long, 1,565 mm wide, and 1,635 mm tall, with a 2,460 mm wheelbase.
It’s built on the same dedicated “HEARTECT-e” EV platform as the e Sky, with a single electric motor that delivers 90 hp (67 kW) and 98 lb-ft (133 Nm) of torque.
articles.lede: The first-generation Ignis went on sale back in 2000 as a three- and five-door hatchback, and in 2016, Suzuki reintroduced it as a compact crossover.

articles.title: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
articles.description: In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.
paragraphs: COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels.
The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world.
Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “ failure ”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “ divided world ”.
There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “ oil-rich nations ”, while others blame Europe’s “ reluctance” to provide more climate finance.
While it is not accurate to say there was “ no agreement” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference.
COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency.
The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days.
An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.
As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect, the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.

Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”.
articles.lede: In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.

articles.title: EU pushes back Tesla ‘Full Self-Driving’ vote meeting again, now set for December 15
articles.description: The EU committee that could approve Tesla's Assisted Driving (FSD) across Europe now meets December 15. A 'no' would void 12 national approvals.
paragraphs: The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned. The meeting is now December 15.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the new date to Reuters. The Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) has already discussed Tesla’s file at two meetings without putting it to a vote.
Two weeks isn’t much on its own. But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.

In late 2025, Tesla told owners the Dutch regulator RDW had “committed” to approving FSD in February 2026. The RDW publicly corrected it. The Dutch approval came on April 10. Tesla then pointed owners to an EU-wide vote on October 6, and the TCMV agenda for that meeting had no vote on it.

Even the new date took a minute to settle. Belgium’s Flanders transport ministry first said the meeting had moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified it’s December 15. Nobody has given a reason for the change.

And a meeting isn’t a vote. The committee can discuss the file again and push the decision into 2027. Elon Musk said on Tesla’s Q3 call in October that he’d be surprised if EU-wide approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.
EU-wide approval needs at least 15 of the 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU’s population.

Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval so far: the Netherlands, Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, last week, Italy, where Tesla has started the rollout. Using Eurostat population figures, we count those 12 at roughly 29% of the EU’s population.

Germany is the obvious next yes. Berlin got Tesla to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe and then cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in exchange for its support. That would bring the yes camp to about 47%.

So Tesla still needs France, or both Spain and Poland, to get over 65%. Not a sure thing. Sweden asked the EU in June to reject the system unless Tesla removed the ability to drive above the posted limit at all.
articles.lede: The EU committee that could approve Tesla's Assisted Driving (FSD) across Europe now meets December 15. A 'no' would void 12 national approvals.

articles.title: Ireland approves 1,367 MW of solar in sixth renewables auction
articles.description: Ireland’s sixth onshore renewables auction (RESS 6) provisionally greenlit a total of 1,367 MW of solar across 22 projects.
paragraphs: Ireland’s grid operator EirGrid has published the provisional results of the sixth onshore Renewable Electricity Support Scheme auction (RESS 6). As in previous years, solar dominated this auction, with 1,367.24 MW of PV provisionally approved across 22 projects.
In comparison, just 188.05 MW of onshore wind was provisionally successful across six projects.
On paper, RESS 6 results show an increase compared with the 860 MW provisionally approved as part of RESS 5 in September 2025.

A total deemed energy quantity of 1,894.04 GWh was provisionally successful in RESS 6, with solar’s portion of this coming in at 1,317.48 GWh. Just under 1 TWh – 977.67 GWh – of solar was provisionally unsuccessful.
Four RESS 6 projects did not qualify in this year’s auction, all of which were solar. Thirteen projects withdrew – six solar and seven wind.
Most of the provisionally successful solar projects are in the east of the country, near where the country’s first utility-scale solar farm was switched on in 2022, in County Meath.
Irish developers Soleire Renewables and Harmony Solar were the most prolific developers by project capacity named.

Solar Ireland CEO Ronan Power pointed out that although the auction’s outcome was positive, more solar capacity could have been successful if the unsuccessful projects were included. Power said Ireland said effectively “said no to a further 1 GW of solar capacity”, turning down an opportunity to get more renewables on the grid.

But Power also emphasized that the results are still provisional and subject to final approval and implementation. “The priority now must be to turn provisional awards into renewable electricity projects on the ground. We should judge the outcome not only by the capacity awarded, but by the capacity that is ultimately built and connected. The longer-term success of the auction will depend on whether the projects awarded support can secure finance, connect to the grid and reach construction. We also need to understand what happened to the projects that were unsuccessful or withdrawn, particularly as the current framework places significant cost and risk on developers.”
RESS 6 results are due to be finalized on Dec. 9, with notice of awards scheduled for Jan. 11, 2027.
articles.lede: Ireland’s sixth onshore renewables auction (RESS 6) provisionally greenlit a total of 1,367 MW of solar across 22 projects.

articles.title: Italy awards 16 GWh of battery storage in second auction
articles.description: Italy's second Electricity Storage Capacity Procurement Mechanism (MACSE) auction awarded all 16 GWh of capacity offered for delivery in 2029, with a weighted average price 12% below the level recorded in the previous auction.
paragraphs: Italy’s second Electricity Storage Capacity Procurement Mechanism (MACSE) auction, for delivery in 2029, awarded all 16 GWh of capacity on offer across 16 battery energy storage system (BESS) projects, averaging 1 GWh each.

The results are detailed in the auction report published by Italian grid operator Terna. The outcome points to strong participation from market operators and greater price competition than expected. Initial industry reactions have been marked by disbelief, and a full analysis is not yet available. The results appear to indicate a highly competitive market, with awards concentrated among a smaller group of developers, creating challenges for projects that were not selected.
Terna said around 67 GWh of new projects had qualified for the auction, while submitted bids totaled approximately 43 GWh – nearly three times the 16 GWh procurement requirement.

Projects representing the 27 GWh of submitted capacity that was not awarded now have fewer options. They can seek revenue in the merchant market, pursue tolling agreements or rely on Italy’s capacity market. A recent revision of capacity-market rating and derating coefficients will also affect projects in southern Italy. For a battery with a four-hour energy-to-power ratio, the capacity recognized for auction purposes, known as probabilistic available capacity (CDP), is 51% in the Center-South region and 21% in the South, Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia.

The second MACSE auction confirms market interest in developing electrochemical energy storage in Italy. As renewable generation expands, flexible capacity is becoming increasingly important to the power system. The source also points to geopolitical tensions as a factor making electrification an increasingly necessary industrial choice.

The Center-South region recorded the lowest marginal and weighted average premiums, both at €10,716/MWh-year. The South and Calabria region recorded the highest, with a marginal premium of €12,792/MWh-year and a weighted average premium of €11,575/MWh-year.

The largest BESS project selected in the second MACSE auction was a 3,399 MWh installation in the South and Calabria region developed by Enel Produzione. Enel Produzione secured a total of 7,337 MWh, almost half of the overall capacity awarded. A2A Storage followed with 2,244 MWh, while A2A Energiefuture secured a further 364 MWh.

Other major awardees included BESS by Erry, with 1,667 MWh in the South and Calabria region, and Field Melfi, with 1,138 MWh in the same region. Other selected developers included ACL SPV 2, Five-E Italy Orange 2, Nardò Solar Energy, PVexo Apollo 2, Saturn and W Selargius.

articles.title: Hyperscaler emissions are soaring. Do they need better climate goals?
articles.description: Meta is re-evaluating long-held 2030 goals, while Amazon is adopting a new metric entirely.
paragraphs: As their greenhouse gas emissions soar, two of the biggest tech companies in the world are changing how they measure climate and sustainability goals: Meta is re-evaluating long-held 2030 goals, and Amazon is adopting a still-ill-defined “carbon intensity” measure.

Big tech companies for years maintained ambitious net-zero pledges, championing clean energy power purchase agreements, investing in carbon removal and debating the best approach to carbon accounting. But the AI boom has overwritten all of those priorities, and as a result, emissions have skyrocketed as hyperscalers race to secure power for more compute, much of it generated in dirtier parts of the country’s electric grid or from planned off-grid gas-burning turbines.
According to Louise Bammel, a corporate accountability researcher at the nonprofit NewClimate Institute, existing climate pledges are out of step with this new world.
“Both Meta and Amazon are massively expanding new gas power plants, so the question arises if and how realistic it is that their emissions will fall,” Bammel said.

The latest sustainability report from Meta, released last week, showed a roughly 45% increase in net carbon emissions from the previous year, an increase so substantial that the report’s authors said that they are reassessing climate targets.

“We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline and interim milestone,” Meta told Latitude Media in a statement. “We’ll continue investing in emissions reductions and reporting our progress annually.” A Meta spokesperson added that the company will continue to focus on clean energy procurement and more efficient design to address emissions, and aims to provide an update on its plans within the year.

Meta reported 21.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent last year in its total emissions inventory, and 11.8 million metric tons in net emissions after including other factors that reduce carbon dioxide output.

Meanwhile, Amazon, which reported a 16% emissions increase in its most recent sustainability report, announced last week a new sustainability target built on a measure of the carbon intensity of its energy use. The company said its new aim is to reduce the carbon dioxide per unit of energy used by 65% by 2030, compared to 2019 levels.

Chris Roe, director of worldwide carbon at Amazon, told Latitude Media that the company is still committed to reaching net zero by 2040. Amazon also still backs The Climate Pledge, which it co-founded in 2019 and has encouraged more than 700 companies to adopt net-zero goals. But the AI boom has Amazon’s emissions heading in the wrong direction, and fast. Like Meta, the company has embraced fossil fuels, and is poised to become one of the world’s largest users of behind-the-meter gas.

“We’ve always said that our path to net zero by 2040 will not be linear, and here we are,” Roe said. He laid out an argument for “good growth” that makes carbon intensity a tool to decouple emissions growth from economic growth.
articles.lede: Meta is re-evaluating long-held 2030 goals, while Amazon is adopting a new metric entirely.

articles.title: The truth about data centers and electricity prices
articles.description: A conversation with Long Lam and Natalie Northrup of the Brattle Group.
paragraphs: Are data centers raising everyone else’s electricity rates? The extremely unsatisfying answer is, it depends. A new report puts numbers on it: depending on circumstances, a large new load can cut other customers’ rates as much as 6 percent or raise them as much as 9 percent. The good news is that most of what makes the difference is under regulators’ control. I talk with authors Long Lam and Natalie Northrup about the tools available, from minimum bills to “bring your own power.”

According to the polls, Americans are quite angry at data centers for raising their electricity prices. But … are data centers raising their electricity prices? If you’ve paid attention to the ongoing research and analysis around this question, you’re probably aware that the answer is an extremely unsatisfying “it depends.”

A new report from the Brattle Group and the Energy Systems Integration Group tries to put some meat on the bones of that “it depends.” Its authors modeled one enormous new load hooking up to the grid under dozens of scenarios. Depending on the circumstances, that same load either cut everyone else’s rates by around 6 percent or raised them by roughly 9 percent.

What determines whether costs go up or down? It’s mostly stuff we have under our control: whether the grid has spare capacity, whether the big customer shows up as promised, and the rules governing what big new loads pay. The report puts rough numbers on each effect, across four very different US power markets. It’s quite clarifying.

My guests today are the report’s lead author, Long Lam, and his co-author Natalie Northrup, both at The Brattle Group. Long works on load growth, from forecasting to tariffs; Natalie studies how flexible resources make money in power markets.

Many state governments and the US Congress are arguing over who pays for data centers. It’s a big element in the much-discussed federal permitting bill. So it seems like a good moment to help all you Volts listeners get a somewhat more sophisticated understanding of just when data centers hurt the rest of us ratepayers, and when they help. Let’s get into it.
PJM Filing - Interim Resource Adequacy Service and Large Load Registry (FERC Docket ER26-3515)
Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission - Order on NIPSCO and GenCo Data Center Special Contract (Cause No. 46322)
David Roberts: With no further ado, Long Lam, Natalie Northrup, welcome to Volts. Thank you so much for coming.

David Roberts: All right. Long, let’s start with you. You have been studying this basic issue for a while now. There was a big Lawrence Berkeley National Lab report around this a couple of years ago that made a big impression. Talk a little bit about your history with this issue and why this report now.

articles.title: UtmoLight, UNSW achieve 19.6% efficiency for 2.81 m² perovskite solar module
articles.description: The reported result corresponds to a power output of around 551 W and represents a 15% relative efficiency increase over UtmoLight’s previous benchmark. The module was tested at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).
paragraphs: Chinese perovskite solar module manufacturer UtmoLight and researchers from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) in Australia have reportedly achieved a stabilized power conversion efficiency of 19.6% for a single-junction perovskite solar module measuring 2.81 m².

According to technical documentation seen by pv magazine, the result was obtained through maximum power point tracking (MPPT) tests conducted at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).
The reported full-area efficiency corresponds to a power output of approximately 551 W under standard test conditions.

The result represents an improvement of 2.56 percentage points over UtmoLight’s previous efficiency benchmark for modules of comparable size, equivalent to a relative efficiency increase of around 15%.

Maintaining high power conversion efficiencies while increasing module size remains one of the main challenges in the commercialization of perovskite photovoltaics. Large-area module fabrication requires precise control of thin-film uniformity, crystallization, defect passivation, electrical interconnections, and interface quality.
The collaboration combines UNSW’s expertise in materials science and device engineering with UtmoLight’s large-area processing and industrial manufacturing capabilities.
Earlier this year, the two partners achieved a certified stabilized efficiency of 23.5% for a 30 cm × 30 cm single-junction perovskite solar submodule with an aperture area of 676 cm².
The researchers eliminated the conventional nickel oxide layer through a fabrication process that enables the direct formation of a hole-selective contact.
The UNSW team subsequently announced plans to scale up the technology to a module area of 2.8 m², targeting a power conversion efficiency of between 18% and 19%.

UtmoLight has been working on the development of commercial-sized perovskite solar modules for several years. In November 2024, the company unveiled a 450 W perovskite solar panel with a power conversion efficiency of 16.1%, an area of 2.8 m², and a dual-glass design.
articles.lede: The reported result corresponds to a power output of around 551 W and represents a 15% relative efficiency increase over UtmoLight’s previous benchmark.

articles.title: Poweroad unveils modular LFP battery system with up to 245.76 kWh of storage
articles.description: Poweroad's new battery storage system is available in high- and low-voltage configurations and features 5.12 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery modules based on CATL cells. The high-voltage version can also be equipped with a 20 kW electric vehicle charger.
paragraphs: Chinese energy storage specialist Poweroad is showcasing a new modular battery energy storage system at the Genera trade show in Madrid, Spain.
Dubbed Meta Node, the system is designed for residential and small-scale commercial and industrial (C&I) applications and is available in both high- and low-voltage configurations.

“Both units are modular and can offer a storage capacity of around 60 kWh by stacking up to 12 battery modules,” Federico Larcher del Río, Poweroad’s country manager for Spain and Portugal, told pv magazine. “The towers can then be connected in parallel to achieve a total capacity of 245 kWh.”

The high-voltage system has an operating voltage range of 172.8 V to 688.8 V and a storage capacity ranging from 20.48 kWh to 61.44 kWh per tower. It features a maximum operating current of 100 A and a nominal operating current of 50 A.
The low-voltage version has an operating voltage range of 43.2 V to 57.6 V and a storage capacity ranging from 5.12 kWh to 61.44 kWh per tower. Its maximum operating current is 200 A.
Both systems utilize the same 5.12 kWh battery module, which relies on LFP cells supplied by Chinese battery manufacturer CATL. The module measures 590 mm x 390 mm x 133 mm and weighs 50 kg.

The manufacturer claims a lifespan of 8,000 cycles. The modules feature a balancing current of 5 A, IP55-rated protection, natural cooling and an operating temperature range of -20 C to 55 C with heating.

The high-voltage battery can also be equipped with an optional 20 kW DC electric vehicle (EV) charging module featuring a CCS2 connector and an output voltage range of 200 V to 500 V. The air-cooled device measures 590 mm x 390 mm x 215 mm and comes with a 3-meter charging cable.
Larcher said the product is being distributed across Europe and that the company is currently expanding its presence in the Spanish market through distributors such as AutoSolar.

“The system is scalable and very versatile when it comes to adding storage capacity,” he said. “If an installation was initially sized for a smaller storage capacity, it can be expanded in the future.”
articles.lede: Poweroad's new battery storage system is available in high- and low-voltage configurations and features 5.12 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery modules based on CATL cells.

articles.title: UK small-scale battery deployment set to double annual record in 2026
articles.description: Deployment data from certification body MCS reveals small-scale battery storage installations in 2026 are close to doubling annual record set in 2026. Policy support expected to fuel further growth in 2027.
paragraphs: UK small-scale battery storage deployment has accelerated in 2026, with the latest data from certification body MCS showing new monthly and annual records.
MCS recorded 73,115 certified battery storage installations to the end of October 2026, up from 41,460 certified installations in 2025.

MCS certification applies to battery storage installations with power output up to 50 kW. While not a legal requirement, certification is typically required by UK energy suppliers to gain access to payments for exporting to the grid.

Monthly certified installations peaked in July 2026 with 9,382 recorded. Nine of the top ten months on record for installations were in 2026, with 4,343 installations in October 2025 the tenth strongest month. Matching the installation rate from 2025 in the final quarter would see 2026 volumes more than double the previous annual deployment record.

The solar attachment rate for UK small-scale batteries was also high. MCS records show around 82% of certified battery storage systems installed in 2026 were also completed at the same time as solar panels.

Rising battery storage installations comes as the UK government rolls out further support for energy efficiency upgrades to homeowners. The recently launched Warm Homes Loan Scheme sees the UK government work with lenders to de-risk finance for energy efficient home upgrades, such as battery storage, to lower the interest rate offered to consumers at the point of sale. Means tested grants are also available for qualifying low-income homes.

More policy support is coming. Battery storage deployment is expected to benefit from new building regulations in England, which begin a phased rollout from March 2027. Under the new Future Homes Standard builders in England will need to meet more stringent energy efficiency standards, which battery storage and solar installations support.
Lisa Cooke, managing director of MCS, predicted that the new building regulations would support further growth for solar and energy storage deployment in UK homes.

“These numbers are only set to increase as the industry, particularly the new build market, prepares to deliver the Future Homes Standard. With this increased demand, the need for quality installations is more apparent than ever,” Cooke said, adding that MCS has redeveloped its installer scheme “putting quality at the heart of everything we do.”

The certification body is also developing a product standard for battery storage. Under the current certification regime, MCS certifies installation businesses and solar products, however it does not yet operate a battery storage product standard.
articles.lede: Deployment data from certification body MCS reveals small-scale battery storage installations in 2026 are close to doubling annual record set in 2026. Policy support expected to fuel further growth in 2027.

articles.title: Afore unveils all-in-one propane heat pump for residential applications
articles.description: The new air-to-water heat pump series features nominal heating capacities ranging from 8.03 kW to 11.75 kW and coefficients of performance of up to 5.70. The systems can achieve an outlet water temperature of up to 75 C.
paragraphs: Chinese inverter and energy storage system manufacturer Afore is expanding its product offering to include residential heating and cooling solutions, with the introduction of a new series of air-to-water heat pumps designed specifically for the European market.

The new products, which rely on R290 (propane) as the refrigerant, are intended for both standalone applications and integration into residential energy systems combining solar power generation, battery storage, and electric vehicle charging.
“The heat pump can be sold independently or as part of a complete system,” Afore Vice General Manager Dong Chen told pv magazine.

Chen explained that, through an external energy management system (EMS) featuring artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, homeowners can optimize electricity consumption based on fluctuations in electricity prices while maximizing the use of solar power and stored energy.
The company offers both single-phase and three-phase heat pumps, with the latter primarily targeting the German market, Chen said.

The new all-in-one system combines an outdoor monobloc heat pump with an indoor hydraulic module integrating a buffer tank, a domestic hot water tank, circulation pumps, valves, expansion vessels, and an intelligent control system.

The series is available in three versions with nominal heating capacities of 8.03 kW, 9.88 kW, and 11.75 kW. Their maximum heating capacities at an outdoor temperature of 7 C and an outlet water temperature of 35 C are 12 kW, 14 kW, and 16 kW, respectively.
Under the same temperature conditions, the systems feature coefficients of performance (COPs) ranging from 4.42 to 5.70. At an outlet water temperature of 55 C, their COPs range from 3.08 to 4.06.
The three models have an energy efficiency rating of A+++ for space heating at 35 C and A++ at 55 C, as well as an A rating for domestic hot water production.
The heat pumps can operate at ambient temperatures ranging from -25 C to 43 C in heating mode and achieve a maximum outlet water temperature of 75 C.
articles.lede: The new air-to-water heat pump series features nominal heating capacities ranging from 8.03 kW to 11.75 kW and coefficients of performance of up to 5.70. The systems can achieve an outlet water temperature of up to 75 C.

articles.title: Belgium forecast to reach 28.6 GW of solar by 2035
articles.description: GlobalData expects Belgium’s solar capacity to more than double from 2025 levels, with distributed installations leading growth amid rising electricity demand and declining nuclear capacity.
paragraphs: Belgium is on track to deploy 28.6 GW of solar by 2035, according to analysis by GlobalData.
Solar is already the largest technology in Belgium’s capacity mix, the UK-based consultancy says, with 12.8 GW of installed capacity in 2025, equivalent to 43.4% of its total.
Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, Power Analyst at GlobalData, told pv magazine he expects Belgium’s solar capacity to grow at a compound annual growth rate of around 8% to 2035.
He explained that as the country’s nuclear fleet contracts, falling to 2.1 GW last year, and with no new reactors committed to, most new supply has to come from renewables.

“Solar is the fastest and lowest-cost option to deploy at scale [while] electricity demand is set to rise as transport, heating and industry electrify,” he explained. “Electric vehicles, heat pumps and the industrial clusters around Antwerp and Ghent will all increase consumption.”
He added that regional policy, such as Flanders’ requirement for rooftop solar on large commercial and public buildings with high electricity use, also continues to support deployment.
Saibasan said the build out of solar will be led by distributed solar systems, which make up most of Belgium’s existing solar fleet, as land for large ground-mounted plants is limited.

“We expect commercial and industrial rooftops to be the strongest segment. The Flemish building mandate, high retail tariffs and corporate demand for on-site clean power all favour self-consumption,” Saibasan said. He added residential growth will continue but more slowly now that net metering has been withdrawn in the regions of Flanders and Wallonia.
Saibasan said grid capacity and revenue stand as the biggest obstacles that could prevent Belgium reaching the 28.6 GW projection.

“Distribution networks were not designed for large volumes of rooftop solar flowing back into the grid, so local congestion and connection delays could slow installations,” he said. “Frequent negative power prices at midday, already a feature of the Belgian market, also reduce the value of uncontrolled solar output and weaken the case for merchant projects.”
articles.lede: GlobalData expects Belgium’s solar capacity to more than double from 2025 levels, with distributed installations leading growth amid rising electricity demand and declining nuclear capacity.

articles.title: German agrivoltaics developer launches free tool for project planning
articles.description: Ylektra has introduced an online calculator to help farmers and project developers assess whether category II systems meet key agricultural requirements under DIN SPEC 91434, a German technical specification for agrivoltaics.
paragraphs: German agrivoltaics project developer Ylektra has published a free online calculator to help users assess, at an early planning stage, whether category II agrivoltaic systems meet key agricultural requirements under DIN SPEC 91434.

The specification defines requirements for maintaining primary agricultural use at agrivoltaic installations. Category II covers low-mounted systems in which farming takes place between the module rows.

Users can enter the site location and crop type, along with system parameters such as row spacing, module height and orientation, and the working width of their agricultural machinery. The calculator covers systems with single-axis trackers and vertically installed bifacial modules. A traffic-light system assesses factors including land-use loss, cultivation access, light availability and expected agricultural yield.

Ylektra says the calculations draw on irradiation data from the European Commission’s Photovoltaic Geographical Information System (PVGIS), research findings from the agrivoltaic pilot plant in Heggelbach, near Lake Constance in Germany, and a meta-analysis by the University of Hohenheim covering 58 studies on the effects of shading.

The calculator does not replace detailed system planning or certification. Other requirements under DIN SPEC 91434, including water distribution, soil protection and decommissioning, must be assessed separately.
Ylektra recently published a freely accessible atlas of agrivoltaic projects in Germany. The atlas covers 2,697 projects in 109 countries.

articles.title: Campaign aims to bring solar-plus-storage to 50,000 Indigenous homes
articles.description: Indigenized Energy says solar-plus-storage projects have helped families reduce monthly bills by hundreds of dollars as it launches a $2.5 billion fundraising effort to support a further 50,000 Indigenous homes.
paragraphs: Native-led non-profit Indigenized Energy and international advocacy organisation Global Citizen have kicked off a campaign to bring solar and battery storage to 50,000 homes in Indigenous communities across the U.S. and Canada.

The money raised will go towards developing community-owned solar-plus-storage projects for Indigenous communities that often sit at the end of utility lines, face high costs and power outages that can last for days. It will also go towards developing workforce training and the local capacity required to sustain these systems once operational.

“That includes solar panels and battery storage, plus, where needed, improvements such as appliance upgrades or other measures to make the home more energy efficient,” Romero said. “Actual costs will vary depending on the home, location, and scope of work.”

The number of communities to be the support by the initiative is not fixed, Romero added, but the initiative plans to expand Indigenized Energy’s reach into Canada through partnership with other Native organisations.
Projects are due to commence next year, Romero revealed, with installations in Pine Ridge, South Dakota, and with the Menominee Tribe in Wisconsin already planned.

“Construction in these locations slows during the winter because of cold weather and frozen ground,” she explained. “We use those months to secure funding, coordinate logistics and prepare with our Tribal partners for installations to resume as conditions allow in the spring.”
Romero added that the goal is to reach 50,000 homes over the next seven years, with the pace of installations dependent on funding and readiness in participating communities.
Romero told pv magazine this example is one of several that the organisation hears of once installations are up and running.

“Homeowners consistently report bills dropping within the first few months and remaining low, sometimes reaching zero, depending on the home’s electricity needs and the size of the system,” she said. “Other homeowners who previously experienced frequent outages tell us they now sometimes do not even realise the surrounding community has lost power because their battery keeps their home running.”
Romero added that many of the households that benefit from Indigenized Energy’s solar-plus-storage solutions are part of communities that face significant poverty, with many living on fixed incomes.
articles.lede: Indigenized Energy says solar-plus-storage projects have helped families reduce monthly bills by hundreds of dollars as it launches a $2.5 billion fundraising effort to support a further 50,000 Indigenous homes.

These Maine heat-pump owners will get discounted power this winter
articles.description: A top utility has rekindled a program that could save heat pump owners hundreds of dollars a year — and nudge more residents to ditch pricey heating oil.
paragraphs: A discount electricity rate for heat pump owners in Maine seemed dead earlier this year. Now, it’s been revived as regulators look for ways to encourage households to ditch increasingly pricey heating oil and make winter warming more affordable for those already using the electric systems.

The Maine Public Utilities Commission last week approved the rate structure proposed by the state’s top electric utility, Central Maine Power, which serves more than 670, 000 households across most of the western half of the state. CMP expects the voluntary program, which kicks in Dec. 1, to save participating customers hundreds of dollars annually compared to default rates.

The heat pump rate eliminates transmission and distribution charges during the winter, leaving customers to pay for their electric supply — 13. 63 cents per kilowatt-hour as of the new year — and a monthly fee of about $ 41 (somewhat higher than the $ 27 monthly fee paid by standard-rate households). Customers who opt into this rate will then see a higher rate during the summer months: 25 cents per kWh, as opposed to the standard rate’s 12 cents per kWh.

The idea is that the savings from winter operations will be greater than the additional summer costs, giving customers a net financial advantage. A customer who uses 500 kWh per month in the summer and 1, 200 kWh per month in the winter would save $ 211 per year, compared to standard rates, according to CMP’s calculations. Use less in the summer and more in the winter and the savings go up.
Having these savings available also amplifies the case for switching from oil heat to heat pumps, supporters of the rates say.

CMP originally launched the heat pump rate as a pilot at the beginning of 2023. It expired on Jan. 31, 2026, and was not extended, following a study that found the offering did not create significant savings for customers or motivate meaningful changes in how much power participants used.

Now, however, circumstances have changed. The price of heating oil — used by roughly half the homes in Maine — has spiked as a result of the ongoing war in the Middle East, lingering just below $ 6 per gallon in recent weeks. Heat pumps and the accompanying discount rates could offer much-needed savings this winter, regulators reasoned in their decision approving the new pricing structure. Essentially, the heat pump rate is just more likely to drive heat pump adoption at this point than during the pilot, supporters argued during the approval process.

“ The cost of delivered fuels is incredibly high right now,” said Alex Lopez, senior manager of regulatory policy at electrification nonprofit Rewiring America, which was not directly involved in the Maine decision. ​ “ Heat pumps represent an opportunity to upgrade heating systems with a fuel that is less volatile, more efficient, provides healthier indoor air quality … there’s just so many benefits.”

Heat pump rates are gaining traction in other cold-winter places as well. Massachusetts requires all three of its major electric utilities to offer a lower seasonal rate for heat pump users, which took effect last winter. In that first season, the rates saved customers more than $ 37 million, an average of more than $ 250 per household. In Minnesota, Xcel Energy offers a program that lowers seasonal rates for homes with electric heat — both heat pumps and resistance. Colorado utilities will be required to consider heat pump discounts in future rate requests, and New York is looking at whether it can alter its current time-of-use rates to create more savings for heat pump users.
articles.lede: A top utility has rekindled a program that could save heat pump owners hundreds of dollars a year — and nudge more residents to ditch pricey heating oil.

articles.title: Uber drivers are flocking to EVs amid high gas prices
articles.description: The world’s largest ride-hailing app is seeing record EV growth among U.S. drivers, a bright spot for the country’s floundering electric vehicle market.
paragraphs: U.S. electric vehicle sales fell off a cliff last year after Republicans deleted the federal EV tax credit. But sky-high gasoline prices are causing EV adoption to soar among one of the populations most exposed to fuel costs: Uber drivers.

The ride-hailing company tracks EV adoption on its platform to measure progress toward a corporate goal to reach 100 % electric by 2030 in the U.S., Canada, and Europe. Uber is not on track to hit that ambitious timeline, but a striking trend has emerged from the latest data: Uber drivers in the U.S. and Canada made a smaller share of rides in EVs in the last quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of this year. But from April through September, U.S. Uber drivers set consecutive monthly records for miles driven electric, said Santosh Rao, the company’s global head of mobility electrification.

The U.S. and Israel launched their war with Iran at the end of February, prompting Iran to close the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation. The loss of this key energy supply line rippled through the global market. As the blockade continued, even the U.S.’s world-leading oil production couldn’t shield its drivers from price spikes in this globalized commodity. Domestic average gasoline prices broke $ 4 per gallon at the end of March, according to AAA, and have stayed above that for almost all the year since.

Uber can’t command its drivers to pick a certain vehicle — they are independent contractors, after all. Its EV data reflects the aggregated decisions of millions of individuals making economic choices about their livelihood. As gas prices ticked higher, the people who routinely fill up a tank once or more per day felt it the hardest, and for six months running, more of them chose electric driving than ever before.

EV advocates and researchers have long argued that the total cost of ownership favors EVs even if they have a higher sticker price than a comparable combustion-engine model. That total cost metric calculates fuel savings over time as well as cheaper maintenance — fewer moving pieces, no oil changes, etc.
The math works out for many Uber drivers. Rao added that, in addition to lower operating costs, electric cars offer smoother and better rides for Uber customers.

But not everyone can spend more up front with an expectation to save money in the long run. The haywire fossil fuel markets, however, made the short-term pain of gasoline dependency so acute that it pushed Uber drivers into cleaner vehicles. It’s as if President Donald Trump’s elective military intervention created an unintended carbon tax.
U.S. Uber drivers chose electric cars for one in 10 miles driven as of September. In Europe, which bought more EVs in September than ever before, EVs traversed one in 5 miles driven on the platform.

Globally, the quarterly count of zero-emission Uber trips rose 34 % since the first quarter, to 207 million trips. And Uber now hosts 434, 000 EV drivers, up 28 % since the Q 1 report — compare that with the total 10. 8 million active drivers and couriers Uber reported in the third quarter (though the electrification reporting tracks only ride-hail drivers, not couriers). A few cities lead the pack: EV miles driven on Uber are now over 50 % in Amsterdam, over 40 % in London, and over 35 % in Vancouver.
articles.lede: The world’s largest ride-hailing app is seeing record EV growth among U.S. drivers, a bright spot for the country’s floundering electric vehicle market.

articles.title: Why everyone is talking about grid utilization
articles.description: The push to get more out of the grid is picking up momentum.
paragraphs: The grid is built to serve peaks on the hottest afternoon or coldest morning of the year. The rest of the time, much of that capacity is unused. So how do we use more of it to accommodate load growth?

A growing coalition of experts argues that the US electric system has vast untapped potential, hidden in the underutilized infrastructure we’ve already built. And they’re pushing utilization as a resource that utilities can harness.

This fall, that idea became concrete. Under a first-of-a-kind law, Virginia required its two biggest utilities to file utilization metrics with regulators. Supporters say it will provide more visibility into parts of the system that can accommodate more power, and change the way utilities plan and build.

This week, a deep dive into the concept of utilization: how it works, why it matters, and where it fits into the growth of the grid. This conversation was recorded live at Latitude Media’s Flex Summit in Austin, Texas.

Stephen sits down with Molly Knoll, a senior advisor at Align Energy Advisors; Ian Magruder, founder and executive director of the Utilize Coalition; and Zach Zimmerman, director of research at Grid Strategies. They discuss how utilization should be defined, reflect on lessons learned from Virginia, and explore critiques of the approach.

Open Circuit is brought to you by EnergyHub. EnergyHub works with more than 230 utilities to coordinate over 2.6 million DERs and more than 3.6 gigawatts of dispatchable flexibility through a single platform designed to perform when it counts most. See what that looks like at EnergyHub.com.

Open Circuit is brought to you by Everyday Electric. Everyday Electric simplifies savings at home, helping support a more reliable, affordable grid. Operating the country’s largest residential VPP, it coordinates 6+ GW of capacity across connected products. Learn more at everydayelectric.com.

Molly Knoll: I talked to a distribution system engineer and I said, “Look, how many more kilowatt-hours can we flow through the system? If we control peak and we raise the valley, how much more value can we get out of the existing grid?” And there’s just silence on the other end of the phone. The guy was like, “Why would you even ask that question?” I said, “Because that’s how we drive down rates for customers. That’s how we handle electrification of transportation and buildings.” And when we talk about utilization, I really want to be talking about durable solutions that go beyond the data center moment to the load growth that’s coming in the five and 10 years beyond that.

Stephen Lacey: Policymakers are desperate to contain rising rates, and do it without choking off economic growth. So they’re increasingly looking at how to make better use of the grid we’ve already paid for. And utilization has become the concept of the moment in the power sector. It’s a pretty simple concept. We build the grid for the hottest afternoon and the coldest morning of the year, and then much of it sits idle the rest of the time. If you can get more power through those wires, you can connect new load faster and spread the cost of the grid over more kilowatt-hours. And now it’s moving into actual policy, first in Virginia and likely soon in other states. So is there a common playbook emerging, and what are the limits? This week on Open Circuit, a conversation with the people pushing utilization forward and the hard questions they’re still working through.
articles.lede: The push to get more out of the grid is picking up momentum.

articles.title: Is it time for oil and gas to lean in on next-gen geothermal?
articles.description: The industry has momentum thanks to both federal policy and the AI boom. Now, experts say, it needs fossil fuel money.
paragraphs: About 20 miles southeast of Bend, Ore., hot rocks lurk below the surface of cauldron-like hills and an expansive obsidian formation. The area, known as the Newberry Volcano, is a major testing ground for enhanced geothermal systems due to its extreme underground heat.

They told Latitude Media that whether the industry can unlock power at gigawatt scale in the coming years likely relies on several major breakthroughs: how Fervo’s Cape Station performs; whether Congress can pass permitting reform that yields much faster timelines for building big energy projects like transmissions lines — critical infrastructure to the geothermal industry — and whether the oil and gas industry brings in massive balance sheets.

Research analysts at Bank of America made a similar observation in a Nov. 20 note to investors. While startups have accelerated innovation, they said, delivering multiple gigawatts on shorter timelines will likely require greater investment from oil and gas majors.

If one or more major fossil fuel company commits to a multi-GW project for a large power buyer, that could validate the market and accelerate investment across the supply chain, the note said, which summarized a call with Jamie Beard, founder and executive director of Project InnerSpace, a geothermal research nonprofit.

But investors are still wary. Fervo’s stock dropped about 70% since its debut in May amid concerns about the massive capital needed to expand its first commercial plant in Utah, called Cape Station, which delivered its first 33 megawatts of power in September.

Transmission bottlenecks are also undercutting confidence in the market. And companies are still testing a wide range of different ESG technologies to unlock geothermal power in more geological formations than past approaches that were limited to naturally occurring hotspots.

As a result, the sector remains a risky bet for traditional infrastructure investors. It instead relies on a mix of venture capital, strategic power purchase agreements with hyperscalers and utilities, and DOE grants, according to Rebecca Rogers, a partner at law firm Foley Hoag who advises on renewable and geothermal project finance.

“Project finance hates uncertainty, and they hate variation because it leads to uncertainty,” Rogers told Latitude Media. “This is still largely wildcatting. You have to pick a 30-square-foot location and punch a hole in the ground. That’s a really costly decision.”

Fervo followed a similar financing pathway up until its IPO in May. Cohen of Currence said the nearest term bellwether for the industry is what happens at Fervo’s Cape Station as it expands over the next couple years. Data on drilling costs, repeatability, and sustained thermal output will be closely watched — and ultimately will likely determine whether EGS can attract bigger pools of capital, especially from oil and gas majors.

“How it performs in the first year or two will really indicate how many people are going to rush in with how much capital, how fast,” Cohen said. “Anything before those data points, you’re kind of like, is EGS something that’s kind of cool and will improve over a long time, or will there be a flip much sooner, where those oil majors come in each doing gigawatt-sized [projects]? Those things are up in the air.”
articles.lede: The industry has momentum thanks to both federal policy and the AI boom. Now, experts say, it needs fossil fuel money.

France may tie 5.5% solar VAT rate to RG5 hail resistance
articles.description: A forthcoming French decree could require RG5 hail-resistant modules and qualified installation for residential PV systems up to 9 kW to qualify for the reduced 5.5% value-added tax (VAT) rate.
paragraphs: France is preparing to introduce stricter technical and installation requirements for residential solar systems seeking the reduced 5.5% VAT rate, including RG5 hail-resistance certification for modules and installation by a qualified professional, according to the National Federation of Solar Energy (FNES).
The new decree, which is expected to be published shortly, would introduce RG5 as a requirement for photovoltaic installations eligible for the reduced tax rate.

RG5 is the highest level of hail resistance in the European classification, including the AEAI-VKF hail register. It certifies that a material or product, such as a roof tile, facade component or solar panel, can withstand impacts from hailstones at least 50 mm in diameter, traveling at around 100 to 110 km/h, without visible damage or loss of function.

The requirement would represent a significant increase over the standard IEC 61215 module certification, which tests resistance to hailstones measuring 25 mm in diameter. For hailstones of the same shape, doubling the diameter increases their mass eightfold.

Against a backdrop of more frequent hail events and growing reluctance among insurers to cover exposed installations, the proposed requirement could exclude many modules currently eligible for the reduced VAT rate. The French manufacturer Voltec Solar’s Tarka L11OR 500 W module, in its Diamant version, is cited as a notable exception.

For installers and distributors, the timing is significant because the new rules could take effect the day after publication. Subject to any transitional provisions for sales already agreed, modules without RG5 certification would no longer qualify for the reduced rate.

For quotations already accepted at the 5.5% rate, FNES recommends that installers collect initial deposits without delay and check that modules have valid certification. Installers should also ask suppliers which module models hold RG5 certification to prepare for future sales.

The decree of Sept. 8, 2025, which extended the 5.5% VAT rate to residential solar installations of up to 9 kW from Oct. 1, 2025, already imposed several conditions. These included a module carbon footprint below 530 kg of CO2 equivalent per kW, limits on silver, lead and cadmium content, and an energy management system.
The forthcoming decree would add installation by a qualified or certified company and introduce tighter checks on carbon-footprint calculations and measures to combat fraud.

How does EIA compare different types of energy?
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Note: Btu=British thermal units To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren’t combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity.

For combustible fuels, EIA uses thermal conversion factors to convert the physical units into heat content values. Because these factors can change based on the specific characteristics of fuels being produced at different points in time, we update our conversion factors each year.

We publish heat content data for more than 30 petroleum products, 4 types of coal, and natural gas. Each fuel has a unique chemistry and heat content, and the heat content can vary based on the different types of fuel in the mix. For example, the heat content of anthracite coal is higher than the heat content of lignite. The aggregate heat content of coal generally varies based on the mix of the different types of coal produced and consumed.

The aggregate heat contents for petroleum consumption and production have declined in recent decades because of decreasing use of residual fuel oil, which has relatively high heat content, and increasing use of fuels with a lower heat content—such as motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and hydrocarbon gas liquids.

Our heat content estimates for natural gas have fluctuated within a relatively narrow range because of highly consistent pipeline specifications. Methane, the primary component of natural gas, has a heat content of 1,010 Btu per cubic foot. Other gases such as ethane, biomass gases, synthetic gases, and supplemental gases, which may be left in the natural gas stream, have higher heat content values.

Total coal thermal conversion factors depend on the relative mix of coal types consumed and produced that year. Anthracite and bituminous coals have higher heat contents than lignite and subbituminous coals. Subbituminous coal production and consumption have increased over time, bringing down coal’s aggregate heat contents.

To measure how efficient a power plant is at converting the fuel into electricity, we use heat rates. While thermal conversion factors measure the heat content of a fuel, heat rates measure the efficiency of power plants to convert fuel into heat and then into electricity. The heat rate is the amount of energy used to generate one kilowatthour (kWh) of electricity. The lower the heat rate, the higher the efficiency of a power plant to convert fuel into electricity.

Since 2001—the earliest year in our data—heat rates for electricity generation from coal and petroleum have risen slightly, while the heat rate for electricity generation from natural gas has gone down, due in part to more efficient combined-cycle plants coming online.

Algeria’s solar capacity surpasses 1 GW
articles.description: Analysis by Rystad Energy finds that Algeria has added 760 MW of solar capacity this year following the commissioning of three major projects. International financing, grid expansion and regular procurement rounds will be key to achieving its 15 GW renewables target by 2035.
paragraphs: Algeria’s installed solar capacity has exceeded 1 GW, according to analysis by Rystad Energy.

The country has inaugurated three large-scale solar projects this year, the latest of which, the 300 MW El Oued Foulia solar plant, is now its largest operational PV facility. These three plants have added 760 MW of solar already this year, Rystad Energy says, more than Algeria had installed in total by the end of last year.

Surpassing the 1 GW milestone marks a step toward Algeria’s target of deploying 15 GW of renewables by 2035. Work continues on the first phase of the country’s renewables program, which covers 3.2 GW of solar capacity.

Algeria’s next interim target is to add a further 2 GW of solar capacity in 2027. Nivedh Thaikoottathil, Senior Analyst, Renewables & Power at Rystad Energy, told pv magazine the target is achievable as it is supported by an existing project pipeline rather than new projects that still need to be tendered.

“Government-led procurement with [state-owned utility] Sonelgaz’s 1 GW scheme and a 2 GW tender translated policy ambitions into executable projects,” he explained. “With Sonelgaz being the owner it avoids power purchase agreement (PPA) bankability questions, giving greater speed and certainty.”

Thaikoottathil said meeting next year’s 2 GW target will depend on the timely completion of substations and transmission infrastructure, particularly in southern Algeria, as well as effective coordination between Sonelgaz and engineering, procurement and construction contractors. Equipment supply, customs procedures and local-content requirements could also cause delays, while mobilization and site management in remote areas present additional challenges.

“State-backed procurement reduces commercial uncertainty, while continued funding and project supervision should support delivery,” Thaikoottathil said. “Strong political backing also helps prioritize resources, but it can produce overly optimistic announced completion dates.”
Thaikoottathil suggested that in order to reach the 15 GW by 2035 target, Algeria needs to shift from its state-funded first phase to an externally-financed, regularly-tendered second phase.

“Operational solar PV, along with the 2 GW targeted for 2027, and a 0.2 GW wind tender cover only about 23% of the 15 GW target,” he told pv magazine. “Closing the gap means adding more than 1.4 GW a year from 2028 to 2035.”
Regular, rolling auctions of 1.5 GW to 2 GW will be important to sustaining deployment, alongside standardized PPAs, faster permitting and payment security from Sonelgaz, he added.
articles.lede: Analysis by Rystad Energy finds that Algeria has added 760 MW of solar capacity this year following the commissioning of three major projects.

articles.title: Gokin Solar launches 510 W all-black BC panel with 25.0% efficiency
articles.description: The Chinese manufacturer’s new double-glass, all-black modules are designed for high-end rooftop applications across Europe. They feature a temperature coefficient of -0.26% per C and a 30-year linear power output guarantee.
paragraphs: Chinese solar module manufacturer Gokin Solar has presented a new series of full-black solar panels based on back-contact cell technology at the Genera trade show in Madrid, Spain.

The company’s sales manager for the European region, Gloria Luo, told pv magazine that the new panels were designed primarily for high-end rooftop applications, where both aesthetics and module dimensions are important considerations. “The panels will be available across all European markets,” she said.

The panels rely on the company’s proprietary GBC technology, which utilizes lightly doped, high-resistivity n-type silicon wafers. According to the manufacturer, the cell architecture places all electrodes on the rear side, eliminating front-side metallization shading and increasing the active light-receiving area by around 1.1%.
The GK-3-54HGFDb series comprises five versions with power outputs ranging from 480 W to 510 W and power conversion efficiencies ranging from 23.5% to 25.0%.

All versions of the panel measure 1,800 mm x 1,134 mm x 30 mm and weigh 24.8 kg. They feature 108 cells arranged in a 6 x 18 configuration, two layers of 2 mm coated semi-tempered glass, a black anodized aluminum frame, and an IP68-rated junction box.
Luo said the company is also offering a version of the product with a black frame rather than a full-black design, depending on customer requirements and price considerations.
The open-circuit voltage ranges from 40.44 V to 40.84 V and the short-circuit current is between 14.78 A and 15.18 A.

The panels have a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and a temperature coefficient of -0.26% per C. The temperature coefficients for the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current are -0.22% per C and 0.05% per C, respectively.

The modules can withstand front and rear static loads of up to 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively. They have also undergone hailstone testing with 25 mm diameter hailstones at a speed of 23 m/s, according to the datasheet.

The new products come with a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year linear power output guarantee. The modules are guaranteed to retain 99% of their nominal power output after the first year and 88.85% after 30 years, corresponding to an annual degradation rate of 0.35% after the first year.
articles.lede: The Chinese manufacturer’s new double-glass, all-black modules are designed for high-end rooftop applications across Europe. They feature a temperature coefficient of -0.26% per C and a 30-year linear power output guarantee.

articles.title: Felicity Solar showcases 20 kWh low-voltage residential battery
articles.description: The Chinese manufacturer’s new lithium iron phosphate battery features a maximum charging power of 10.2 kW, a maximum discharging power of 12.8 kW, and a depth of discharge of 95%. Up to 15 units can be connected in parallel for a total storage capacity of 300 kWh.
paragraphs: China-based battery manufacturer Felicity Solar unveiled a new low-voltage battery energy storage system for residential and small-scale commercial and industrial (C&I) applications at the Genera trade show in Madrid, Spain.

“This product is for the whole world,” Qiqi Zheng, regional director at Felicity Solar, told pv magazin e, noting that that the adoption of higher-capacity cells is intended to address increasing household electricity consumption.

Dubbed FLA48392TG2-EU, the new product belongs to the company’s FLA series and utilizes lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) cells with a capacity of 392 Ah, providing a nominal energy storage capacity of 20 kWh.

The battery has a nominal voltage of 51.2 V and an operating voltage range of 44.8 V to 57.6 V. Its recommended charging and discharging currents are 100 A and 125 A, respectively, while its maximum charging and discharging currents are 200 A and 250 A, respectively. The system supports a peak current of 300 A for two minutes and has a maximum charging power of 10.2 kW and a maximum discharging power of 12.8 kW.

The floor-mounted battery measures 960 mm x 450 mm x 265 mm and weighs 150.5 kg. It features an IP21-rated enclosure and a depth of discharge of 95%. Its operating temperature ranges from 0 C to 55 C during charging and from -20 C to 55 C during discharging.

The system integrates a battery management system (BMS), a fuse, a circuit breaker, and an aerosol-based fire suppression system. Zheng said the battery, like the company’s other storage products, incorporates multiple levels of protection and features LED and LCD displays that allow users to monitor the battery’s state of charge (SOC).

The device also supports CAN 2.0, RS485, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth communication. “It can be 15 units in parallel,” Zheng said, referring to the system’s scalability to 300 kWh, which also makes it suitable for small-scale C&I installations.

The regional director noted that the company has already deployed multiple units of its existing 16 kWh low-voltage battery in parallel in Spain, demonstrating the potential of its residential storage technology for larger-scale applications.

Felicity Solar claims the new battery has a lifespan of at least 10,000 cycles at 25 C. The company offers a 10-year warranty and lists a cumulative energy throughput of 62 MWh, based on a residual capacity of 60% at the end of life.

Founded in 2007 and headquartered in Guangzhou, southern China, Felicity Solar manufactures solar inverters, lithium batteries, and energy storage systems for residential and C&I applications. The company established its first overseas subsidiary in Nigeria in 2016 and expanded into the European market in 2022, with operations in Germany and the Netherlands.
articles.lede: The Chinese manufacturer’s new lithium iron phosphate battery features a maximum charging power of 10.2 kW, a maximum discharging power of 12.8 kW, and a depth of discharge of 95%.
