articles.title: Differ Power unveils ‘9-in-1’ solar-storage heat pump
articles.description: The Chinese company has developed a residential heat pump system integrating a 6 kW hybrid inverter and supporting battery storage. The propane-based system comes in three versions with heating capacities ranging from 12 kW to 16 kW and can deliver hot water at temperatures of up to 75 C.
paragraphs: Differ Power has unveiled a “9-in-1” air-to-water heat pump system for residential applications at Spain’s Genera trade show. The system combines space heating, cooling and domestic hot water production with PV power inversion, battery management, a power conversion system (PCS), backup power supply, a home energy management system (HEMS) and communication gateway functionality.
Dubbed D Series, the new product was specifically designed for the European residential market and integrates a single-phase hybrid inverter directly into the heat pump unit.

“The most obvious feature is that we put the hybrid inverter inside the heat pump,” Differ Power’s European Product and Technical Director, Schaochen Ji, told pv magazine. “The biggest problem for inverters is ventilation.”

Ji explained that the integration enables the inverter to benefit from the heat pump’s ventilation system, reducing thermal stress on its electronic components and potentially extending its operational lifetime.
“For a 6 kW inverter, heat is no longer a problem. The lifespan of the inverter will be significantly extended,” he added.

According to Ji, the system was conceived to address the growing convergence of residential PV and heat pump installations in Europe, particularly in the context of building energy efficiency upgrades.
“When you do an energy efficiency upgrade, most of the time you consider the PV installation and the heat pump at the same time. So why not put them together?” he said.
The new heat pump uses propane (R290) as the refrigerant and features a twin-rotary DC inverter compressor, an electronic expansion valve and a brushless DC fan motor.

It comes in three versions with nominal heating capacities of 12.14 kW, 14.02 kW and 16.04 kW at an outdoor temperature of 7 C and an outlet water temperature of 35 C. The coefficient of performance (COP) ranges from 4.57 to 4.82. At an outlet water temperature of 55 C, the heating capacity ranges from 12.16 kW to 15.84 kW, with a COP of between 3.0 and 3.09.

The systems have a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) ranging from 5.06 to 5.11 at an outlet water temperature of 35 C and from 3.96 to 3.99 at 55 C. All three models have an A+++ energy efficiency rating at both temperature levels, according to the manufacturer.
articles.lede: The Chinese company has developed a residential heat pump system integrating a 6 kW hybrid inverter and supporting battery storage.

Pilot line recovers high-purity silver, silicon from PV panels
articles.description: Researchers have tested two routes for separating the layers of end-of-life solar panels on a pilot recycling line, recovering silver and silicon at purities above 99.99% and finding that a shockwave-based process also preserves a layer the heat-based route destroys.
paragraphs: A research team led by academics from Poland’s AGH University of Krakow has found that separating solar panel layers with shockwaves, rather than heat, preserves more material while still yielding high-purity silver and silicon.

Prof. Pradeep Padhamnath of AGH University of Krakow and three collaborators said they recovered silver at above 99.99% purity and silicon at above 99.995% from end-of-life PV panels on pilot recycling lines, using either heat or shockwaves to separate the layers.

The researchers compared a thermal process with electrohydraulic fragmentation (EHF), a shockwave-based separation process. Only EHF recovered the laminating layer around the solar cells completely; the thermal process lost it.
The backsheet, the protective polymer layer on the rear of a module, was recovered at room temperature before the layers were separated.
The scientists also looked at whether EHF could be integrated into an existing PV recycling pilot line, assessing its compatibility and setting out its advantages and challenges.
“Further developments in recycling of polymers and material processing could result in entirely closed-loop recycling of EOL PV panels,” said the research team.

The pilot-line study builds on the group’s 2025 paper in Solar Energy. In that study, the researchers described EHF as a process in which electrodes connected to a power supply of about 50 kV create an arc in water, generating shockwaves that separate the panel’s layers. They tested laboratory-made glass-glass, glass-backsheet and glass-free panels for 240, 480 or 720 seconds.
The group’s earlier work describes the thermal route as heating panels to about 450 C to 550 C to decompose polymers such as EVA, PVDF and PET, separating the glass, metallic ribbons and solar cells.

In the 2025 study, the scientists cited EHF’s room-temperature operation, its lack of toxic emissions and its ability to recover polymers that would otherwise be burned in pyrolysis. They also found the process was sensitive to feed size and could clog when overloaded. EVA did not fully separate from the backsheet, glass-free panels separated poorly, and some fine powder was lost.

The scientists described their latest findings in “ Design of pilot lines with thermal and electrohydraulic fragmentation delamination routes and analysis of materials recovered from end-of-life silicon PV panels ,” which was recently published in Waste Management.

articles.title: Cyprus plans to deploy over 300 MW of battery storage
articles.description: With Cyprus having more than 1 GW of installed solar capacity against average electricity demand of around 650 MW, its government is looking to accelerate storage deployment to address rising solar curtailment and improve grid flexibility.
paragraphs: Cyprus is planning to deploy more than 300 MW of battery storage capacity across its electricity system as it seeks to reduce ongoing curtailment of solar power.

Speaking at the 14th Cyprus Energy Symposium, the country’s Energy, Commerce and Industry Minister Michael Damianos identified energy storage, electricity interconnection and market reforms as the three main pillars of the government’s strategy to address growing pressure on its electricity system.
Damianos told attendees of the symposium that Cyprus has more than 1,040 MW of installed solar capacity, compared with average electricity demand of approximately 650 MW.
This imbalance means the country is forced to curtail renewable electricity during periods of high solar generation while continuing to rely heavily on imported oil.

Solar curtailment in Cyprus hit 47% in 2025 and increased further over the first five months of 2026, reaching 65%. The country’s storage market is still in its relative infancy with its first utility battery project, a 5 MWh facility tied to a 1.8 MW solar array, entering the market in August.
During his speech, Damianos confirmed the first 120 MW of grid-connected storage being developed by the transmission system operator is expected to be operational by summer 2027.

He added that the state-owned utility Electricity Authority of Cyprus is developing 80 MW of storage capacity at its Dhekelia power station, targeted for 2027, and revealed a further 100 MW is planned at Moni power station.
“These investments will reduce renewable energy curtailments, increase system flexibility and allow greater integration of renewables,” Damianos said.
The minister’s speech comes as several battery projects installed earlier this year are still waiting for grid connections in order to begin operations.

Damianos also discussed electricity market reforms designed to encourage more flexible consumption and investment. Cyprus’ competitive electricity market became operational in October 2025, while new rooftop solar installations transitioned from net metering to a market-based self-consumption framework in January this year.

Solar and storage insolvencies hit larger German companies
articles.description: Solar and storage companies accounted for 10 of Germany’s 103 major corporate insolvencies in the third quarter of 2026, with cases increasingly involving project developers and battery manufacturers alongside installers and distributors, according to consultancy Falkensteg.
paragraphs: A total of 103 companies filed for insolvency between July and September, down 3% from the previous quarter and 18% year on year, according to Falkensteg’s quarterly report, published on Monday.

Photovoltaic and storage companies accounted for almost 10% of those cases, a significant increase from two in the second quarter of 2026 and seven in the same period a year earlier. Although the sector recorded 13 major insolvencies in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 16 in the same period of 2025, the size and distribution of the affected businesses have changed.

Alongside installation and trading companies, project developers and battery storage manufacturers are now facing insolvency proceedings. Falkensteg’s analysis found that four of the 10 cases involved solar and wind project developers, three involved battery and storage system manufacturers, and three involved installation and trading companies.

Two of the 10 companies, Enerparc and Varta, each had group revenue exceeding €750 million, making them the largest insolvency cases of the quarter by revenue, Falkensteg said. However, Varta’s residential photovoltaic storage business is not included in its insolvency proceedings.

The reasons for the filings also differed. Varta cited a financing shortfall at its parent company, weaker demand and the loss of a key customer. Enerparc, meanwhile, was unable to secure financing for battery storage projects.

Falkensteg partner Jonas Eckhardt, who authored the report, said the number of cases had fallen but the largest insolvencies had become more significant. While installation companies were particularly affected in 2025, project developers and battery storage manufacturers have increasingly come under pressure in 2026.

Eckhardt said the storage market was expanding rapidly while newly installed photovoltaic capacity had stagnated. Both business models require substantial capital, while revenues can fluctuate considerably. He identified financing as the main constraint, adding that uncertainty over Germany’s planned amendments to its Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) and its grid package was making projects difficult to assess and finance.

Falkensteg expects further major insolvencies in the current quarter. Sonnen and Energiekonzepte Deutschland, among others, filed for preliminary insolvency proceedings in October. However, Eckhardt does not expect the sector to reach its 2025 total of 21 insolvency filings by the end of this year.

articles.title: Residential solar linked to reduced health risks from extreme temperatures
articles.description: Research from Japan finds residential solar installations can offer protection against heat-related mortality by making electricity more affordable for households to run air conditioning.
paragraphs: Residential solar installations can mitigate the mortality risks associated with extremely hot temperatures, according to new research.

Researchers Yi-Chun Ko from the Asian Growth Research Institute and Shinsuke Uchida from Japan’s Doshisha University explored how residential solar can make electricity more affordable to run air conditioning when electricity prices spike due to factors such as supply disruptions, geopolitical shocks or extremely hot weather.

Their findings are presented in the research paper Climate resilience through residential solar energy: Reducing health risks from extreme temperatures, available in the journal Social Science & Medicine. According to Uchida, it marks the “first causal evidence that household solar PV can also work as a public health intervention, reducing heat-related mortality through improved energy affordability”.

Ko and Uchida used the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake as a natural experiment. The shutdown of nuclear power plants following the earthquake contributed to electricity price increases of up to 38%, while Japan simultaneously promoted residential solar PV through a nationwide subsidy program.

The pair combined monthly prefecture-level mortality data from 44 Japanese prefectures between 2009 and 2014 with weather data and official solar installation figures. They then used an instrumental variable approach to isolate the effects of solar PV adoption from other factors that might influence household health outcomes.
The results showed that residential solar PV adoption significantly reduced mortality associated with extreme heat, with the greatest impact observed among people aged 65 and above.

Based on the annual average growth rate of solar PV installations during the study period, the researchers estimated that excess deaths associated with extremely hot days were reduced by approximately 8.2% annually for the overall population and 8.5% for people aged 65 and above.

The protective effects of residential solar were also stronger in warmer prefectures, those that experienced greater electricity price increases following the 2011 earthquake, and areas subject to stricter energy conservation targets. No comparable effects were observed at cold temperatures, which the researchers attributed to solar PV’s stronger generation profile during sunnier and warmer weather.
Analysis from the research paper says these findings “show that distributed renewable energy provides direct health protection during climate extremes”.

“By relaxing households’ electricity affordability constraints, solar PV improves their ability to maintain safe indoor environments when cooling demand is highest,” it explains. “Our findings reframe residential solar PV from a primarily environmental intervention into a multifaceted tool for climate resilience that addresses the interlinked challenges of energy security, public health, and climate adaptation.”
articles.lede: Research from Japan finds residential solar installations can offer protection against heat-related mortality by making electricity more affordable for households to run air conditioning.

articles.title: Rainfall alone cannot eliminate bird-dropping soiling on solar panels, study finds
articles.description: An international research team has found that bird-dropping soiling can cause annual PV performance losses of around 6%. The researchers also found that conventional soiling models underestimate these losses, highlighting the need for improved modeling approaches and cleaning strategies.
paragraphs: An international research team has conducted a year-long experimental study to assess the impact of bird droppings on PV system performance and has found that soiling losses stabilized after a prolonged accumulation period, remaining at consistent levels despite repeated rainfall events.

“Our paper highlights this limitation, but we cannot yet provide a solution,” corresponding author Leonardo Micheli told pv magazine. “Factors such as bird activity and proximity to nesting areas are likely to influence soiling accumulation under these conditions, but further research is needed to identify the quantitative variables that could be used to reliably model this type of soiling.”

“Our study demonstrates that a monitoring approach based on clean irradiance measurements can successfully estimate soiling losses caused by bird droppings, without the need to maintain a clean reference module,” Micheli added. “However, we also show that its accuracy depends on calibration. Furthermore, accuracy could also be influenced by operating conditions, and further validation across different sites is needed to confirm its general applicability.”

“We show that rainfall does not necessarily restore modules to clean conditions: significant soiling losses can persist even after repeated natural cleaning events,” he said. “The existence of this phenomenon has already been discussed in the literature, and our study confirms its relevance in environments affected by bird droppings, as this can be particularly difficult to remove. This challenges the common modelling assumption that rainfall effectively removes accumulated soiling and should be considered when optimizing cleaning schedules and costs. A rainy period should not be taken as evidence that PV modules are free from soiling.”

The experimental setup consisted of two monocrystalline JA Solar JAM54S30-410/MR silicon modules installed at ground level at the University of Split, Croatia. One module served as a clean reference, while the other was left to accumulate natural soiling. Both were mounted on an open rack with identical tilt, azimuth, and height to ensure comparable environmental and irradiance conditions.

The researchers conducted weekly measurements from July 2024 to July 2025. During each session, they recorded four current-voltage (I-V) curves per module using an EKO Instruments MP-11 tracer, while also measuring irradiance and module temperature. Measurements were taken near solar noon under clear skies and stable irradiance conditions, in accordance with IEC 61724-1.

The researchers calculated the soiling ratio by comparing the short-circuit currents of the soiled and clean modules. They also tested an alternative approach that estimates clean-module output using irradiance and temperature data. In addition, they evaluated three established soiling models based on particulate matter concentrations and rainfall. Two models assumed complete cleaning when daily rainfall exceeded 1 mm, while the third accounted for partial cleaning.
articles.lede: An international research team has found that bird-dropping soiling can cause annual PV performance losses of around 6%.

North Carolina utility regulators punt on clean transition tariff
articles.description: The mechanism would allow tech companies to build their own renewables, but the Utilities Commission has dragged its feet on directing Duke to come up…
paragraphs: For big corporations in North Carolina with ambitious climate goals, the clean transition tariff is becoming something of a white whale.

Tech firms and other large electricity consumers have long sought this special rate structure because, across most of the state, they can buy electricity only from Duke Energy, a vertically integrated monopoly utility. A clean tariff would let them contract for their own renewable electrons using Duke as a go-between, without violating the law.

In spring 2024, Duke announced its intention to pursue such a plan but never followed through. Earlier this year, the company said it would evaluate the clean tariff ​ “ in good faith,” but made no commitments.

Last month, the whale got closer than ever, when Duke said it would definitely begin negotiations on a clean tariff in early 2027. Proponents of the policy urged state officials to back up that pledge with an order and an enforceable deadline. They hoped that such a directive would be tucked somewhere in the hundreds of pages of regulatory decisions issued last week.
Instead, the state Utilities Commission, a five-member panel controlled by Republicans, offered encouragement.

“ The Commission declines at this time to direct Duke to file or propose a clean customer tariff,” its Nov. 16 order said. ​ “ The Commission nevertheless recognizes Duke’s representation that it remains willing to collaborate with interested parties. … [It] encourages Duke to work with the interested parties to work on a proposal for a Clean Transition Tariff.”
Steve Levitas, a longtime clean energy lawyer — and, briefly, a commissioner himself — welcomed the verbiage but called it insufficient.

“ This issue is just too important to leave to Duke’s discretion,” said Levitas, now the interim executive director of New Energy Economics, a nonprofit that provides expert testimony in state regulatory proceedings.
Levitas testified this year on behalf of the Corporate Energy Buyers Association, whose 300 -plus business members run the gamut from hospitality to manufacturing to tech companies.
“ All CEBA and many other interveners asked the commission to do was to require Duke to file a new, voluntary customer program,” Levitas said. ​ “ That wasn’t really a huge ask.”
articles.lede: For big corporations in North Carolina with ambitious climate goals, the clean transition tariff is becoming something of a white whale.

articles.title: Japanese utility to forecast perovskite window output with AI
articles.description: Kansai Electric Power has partnered with Panasonic and Kansai University on a two-year trial that will install glass-based perovskite solar modules in campus windows near Osaka and test how accurately an AI platform can predict their output.
paragraphs: Japanese utility Kansai Electric Power has signed a basic agreement with Kansai University, Panasonic Holdings, Panasonic Environmental Engineering, and Kanden Energy Solution to demonstrate Panasonic’s glass-based perovskite solar cells on a working building.

Fourteen modules will be installed in the window frames of a building at the university’s Takatsuki Muse Campus in Takatsuki, Japan’s Osaka prefecture. The partners will collect and analyze generation data under real building and weather conditions, and use the trial to assess installation and operating methods.

Kansai Electric will coordinate the project and use SenaSon, its AI-based energy management service, to forecast the modules’ output from weather and other conditions. It will then compare the forecasts with actual generation to assess their accuracy. The company did not give an accuracy target.

Panasonic Holdings will supply the modules and evaluate their performance, while Panasonic Environmental Engineering will install, operate, and maintain them. Kanden Energy Solution will handle the electrical equipment, and Kansai University will provide the site.
The partners did not disclose the modules’ size, total capacity, transparency, or efficiency. They also did not say whether the electricity will be fed into the grid or used on site.

Kansai Electric began offering SenaSon nationwide in April 2023. The service uses AI forecasts of demand and generation to control distributed resources, such as batteries, electric vehicles, and air-conditioning systems, in real time. The platform is also being used in an AI-led smart energy trial at Osaka Metropolitan University, where it is paired with a vanadium redox flow battery from Sumitomo Electric Industries.

Kansai Electric and Kansai University already have a partnership agreement covering carbon neutrality. Panasonic has tested its glass-based perovskite technology in a building in Fujisawa with Mitsui Fudosan Residential and in office windows made by YKK AP. It began selling glass-based perovskite panels for building-integrated PV ahead of full-scale mass production, which is scheduled to start in April 2029.

Japan aims to deploy around 20 GW of perovskite solar capacity by 2040, and its environment ministry plans to exclude conventional silicon panels from new subsidy programs from fiscal 2027 to prioritize perovskite and other next-generation technologies. Other window trials include a perovskite pilot at Tokyo’s Telecom Center Building, while Ricoh plans to start producing perovskite cells in Japan by 2030.

articles.title: Researchers find up to 2.28% annual wave-induced losses in floating PV systems
articles.description: Researchers in Norway have expanded a modeling framework to assess the impact of wave motion on floating PV performance under realistic weather conditions. Their simulations show that electrical mismatch is the main contributor to energy losses, while changes in average irradiance can produce small gains.
paragraphs: A research team in Norway has expanded a model for wave-induced loss (WIL) in floating photovoltaics (FPV) that it first presented in 2025. The updated framework uses site-specific, time-correlated wave and solar irradiance data to estimate annual energy losses under realistic weather conditions, including cloudy periods.

“While the previous study enabled an understanding of the WIL effect from variations in individual parameters, this work simulates WIL throughout the year, taking into consideration the varying environmental conditions,” the researchers said. “The expanded modeling framework is used to simulate WIL, wave-induced irradiance variation (WIIV), and wave-induced mismatch loss (WIML) for the year 2023 at four nearshore locations along the Norwegian coast.”

The framework consists of four modeling steps. First, in a step added to the original model, the researchers used the SWAN wave model to generate hourly, site-specific sea-state parameters based on wind, boundary wave spectra, and bathymetric data. Second, they used their existing 3DFloat approach to simulate panel movements, assuming that each panel directly follows local wave motion. This step now accounts for changing sea states throughout the year and allows for a more flexible wave spectrum.

In the third step, the researchers used pvlib to calculate the irradiance reaching each moving panel and an equivalent stationary reference panel, accounting for panel orientation and reflection losses. Unlike the previous study, which relied on clear-sky calculations, the updated model uses time-correlated irradiance data that include cloudy periods. Finally, the researchers used the existing PVMismatch electrical model to calculate individual panel and string output, which they integrated over time to determine energy production.

The researchers tested the updated framework through simulations covering the full year of 2023 at four locations along the Norwegian coast, selected to represent increasing exposure to the Skagerrak Strait. The first site is located in a sheltered fjord, while the second is closer to the fjord’s mouth but protected by small islands. The third and fourth sites are located beyond these islands, with the fourth being the most exposed.

At each location, the researchers simulated 10 horizontally mounted panels connected in a single string and arranged along an east-west axis. The electrical parameters were based on Jinko Solar’s Cheetah 60M-V 325 W monocrystalline PERC module, with the panel temperature held constant at 25 C. An additional simulation at the most exposed site used a panel tilt angle of 15 degrees to assess its effect on wave-induced losses.

“The simulations yielded an annual WIL of 1.12% for the most sheltered location (with median wave height 0.22 m) and 2.28% for the more exposed location (with median wave height 0.52 m),” the researchers said. “The contribution from WIML and WIIV was quantified, showing that mismatch losses dominate the total WIL, while changes in average irradiance resulted in a small gain.”
articles.lede: Researchers in Norway have expanded a modeling framework to assess the impact of wave motion on floating PV performance under realistic weather conditions.

articles.title: ECO2 Systems unveils 40 kW CO2 heat pump for commercial hot water applications
articles.description: US-based ECO2 Systems has introduced a new 40 kW air-to-water heat pump for commercial hot water applications. The system uses natural CO2 refrigerant, delivers a heating coefficient of performance (COP) of 5.0 at an ambient temperature of 26.7 C, and can operate at outdoor temperatures as low as -31.7 C.
paragraphs: US-based heat pump water heater manufacturer ECO2 Systems has unveiled a new 40 kW heat pump for commercial domestic hot water applications.
The new Sanco 40kW Heat Pump is designed for multifamily residential buildings, hotels, healthcare facilities, educational institutions and other medium- to large-scale commercial applications.

According to the manufacturer, the system has a nominal heating capacity of 40 kW (136,520 BTU/h) and uses natural CO2 (R744) as its refrigerant. It reportedly achieves a heating coefficient of performance (COP) of 5.0 at an ambient temperature of 26.7 C.
The heat pump can operate at outdoor temperatures ranging from -31.7 C to 45.6 C, making it suitable for installations in cold-climate regions.
The unit measures 1,803 mm × 829 mm × 1,978 mm and has a reported sound level of 57 dBA. It offers a hot water recovery rate of approximately 761 liters per hour at a temperature rise of 50 C.
The system is available with 208/230 V or 460 V three-phase electrical connections, requiring 80 A and 50 A circuit breakers, respectively.

ECO2 Systems said the new heat pump can be installed as a standalone unit or combined with additional units to meet higher hot water demand. It also allows up to 30.5 meters of horizontal separation between the heat pump and storage tanks, including up to 15.2 meters of vertical separation, providing flexibility for commercial system design.
The manufacturer said the product incorporates controls designed to optimize operating performance and support integration with building management systems (BMS).
The new model expands the company’s Sanco2 commercial portfolio, which includes smaller-capacity CO2 heat pumps, hot water storage tanks and control systems.
ECO2 Systems introduced the product as it marks 10 years of Sanco2 operations in North America. The company has not specified a commercial availability date or pricing for the new 40 kW unit.
articles.lede: US-based ECO2 Systems has introduced a new 40 kW air-to-water heat pump for commercial hot water applications.

articles.title: Tongwei unveils oversized solar-plus-storage solution to boost PV capacity credit
articles.description: The system combines substantially oversized PV arrays with battery storage to capture surplus generation and release electricity during periods of higher demand. Tongwei claims the approach could extend annual operating hours to 3,000–4,000 while improving grid connection utilization.
paragraphs: Chinese PV manufacturer Tongwei unveiled its High-Capacity-Credit PV system-level solution on Nov. 18 at the ninth International Photovoltaic and Energy Storage Industry Conference in Chengdu, China.

The proposed system increases DC-side PV capacity to at least twice its original level while retaining the existing grid connection capacity. Battery storage absorbs surplus electricity when solar generation exceeds the plant’s export limit and discharges when PV output falls or demand rises, extending operating hours and shifting generation toward periods of higher electricity demand.

The approach is designed to improve capacity credit, which measures how much of a power plant’s installed capacity can reliably contribute to meeting electricity demand during critical periods. Unlike capacity factor, which reflects electricity generation over time, capacity credit measures a plant’s contribution to grid reliability. The metric is gaining importance in China as the country seeks to make variable renewable generation more dependable.

Tongwei said suitable projects could achieve 3,000 to 4,000 equivalent operating hours annually, compared with approximately 1,000 to 1,500 hours for conventional PV plants. The company also claimed that retrofits could increase investment returns by more than three percentage points under favorable conditions.
Tongwei has not disclosed detailed project economics, the reference capacity used to calculate equivalent operating hours or independently verified operational data supporting the projections.

At the launch, Tongwei signed cooperation agreements with battery manufacturer CATL, inverter and storage supplier Sungrow, the Guangxi branch of China Resources New Energy Investment, Zhongxiang Capital New Energy, Hunan Industrial Equipment Installation and Lingluzhe New Energy.

The partners plan to cooperate on system design, construction, operations and asset securitization for new solar projects and retrofits. Specific investment commitments and equipment orders were not disclosed.

The initiative comes as China’s solar market faces mounting pressure from weaker installations, low midday electricity prices and grid connection constraints. The country added 110.83 GW of PV capacity in the first nine months of 2026, down 53.9% year on year, according to National Energy Administration (NEA) data.

The concept also aligns with China’s 15th Five-Year Plan for Renewable Energy Development, which targets an average dependable capacity contribution of 8% from wind and solar, including approximately 6% for PV, by 2030. New utility-scale wind and solar projects are generally expected to achieve at least 10%, with projects encouraged to exceed 20% where conditions permit.

Tongwei Group Chairman Liu Hanyuan said widespread adoption of the approach could increase grid connection equipment utilization twofold to fourfold, potentially improving project economics while creating additional demand for PV modules, batteries and power electronics.
articles.lede: The system combines substantially oversized PV arrays with battery storage to capture surplus generation and release electricity during periods of higher demand.

articles.title: RE+ was huge this year. Here are 3 solar innovations that stood out.
articles.description: The solar industry’s annual gathering in Las Vegas showcased endless solar panels, batteries, and new technologies illuminating the sector’s next phase of…
paragraphs: LAS VEGAS — It was unusually cool under the desert sun as the U.S. solar industry’s biggest annual convention got underway last week. The live sheep munching hay under a solar display in the convention center parking lot had a layer of wool to keep them warm when the sun dipped behind the looming monorail track. The herds of solar professionals, meanwhile, had to warm themselves with thoughts of the business cycle to come.

After two years in political purgatory, the solar and wind industries saw Americans from coast to coast vote for lawmakers who want to deploy clean technologies to combat rising energy costs. Now, these businesses can look forward to proactive policymaking that could hasten the clean energy transition. But even through the recent hard times, the industries kept building, and now can accelerate to full throttle, like the F 1 drivers that zoomed down the Strip after the solar pros flew home Thursday.

A decade ago, RE +, the industry’s flagship annual event — hosted by the Solar Energy Industries Association and the Smart Electric Power Alliance — was a relatively intimate gathering, where you could, say, follow a plush solar-inverter mascot into a party atop the skyscraping Strat tower and see familiar faces. This fall, for the first time, it was held in the Las Vegas Convention Center, a conglomeration of concrete and steel so sprawling that Elon Musk convinced the city it made sense to drill single-lane subterranean tubes so that chauffeured Teslas could ferry people between the various halls.

Inside, vendors displayed more brands of identical-looking solar panels than anyone could rightly recall. But the convening also featured batteries large and small, grid transformers, electric vehicle chargers, customized electronics packages for smooth data center deployment, and the occasional green hydrogen venture not yet gone out of business.

“ If you look at how broad RE + has become, it’s no longer solar and batteries anymore,” said Raghu Belur, chief products officer at Enphase, the pioneering solar microinverter company. ​ “ It’s all elements that interconnect to a more modern, sophisticated grid.”

Things that would have been shocking five years ago are now commonplace, like booths touting American-made solar and batteries. Claims of compliance with ​ “ foreign entity of concern” rules — which Republicans imposed last year to restrict tax credit eligibility — were ubiquitous on this year’s floor.

Even a thoroughly settled industry must have its frontiers, however, and amid the miles walked under fluorescent lights and the fruitless search for available chairs, I found three technological innovations that, taken together, show us something about where Big Solar is headed next.

Scientists have long contended that crystalline structures called perovskites can propel solar panel efficiency to a whole new level. Now, some companies are taking this tech out of the lab and into the real world. I got my first chance to see it in person in Vegas.
articles.lede: It was unusually cool under the desert sun as the U.S. solar industry’s biggest annual convention got underway last week.

articles.title: Energy companies whiplashed by Nvidia drama as Jensen Huang returns
articles.description: The Nvidia CEO’s personal role in partnerships, including with energy startups, earned him the reputation as “the bank of Huang.”
paragraphs: After 11 days, Jensen Huang is back. The Nvidia CEO had resigned earlier this month after multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. But after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” per a statement from Nvidia’s board — reporting suggests that President Donald Trump made an appearance at Nvidia’s board meeting to lobby for Huang — the CEO made a triumphant return.
“Thank you all for the second chance,” Huang said in a video clip posted to social media as he addressed cheering Nvidia workers. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”
President Trump lobbied hard for Huang’s return, and told CNBC Monday, “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.”

Huang’s return caps off weeks of whiplash for both the technology and energy industries. A combination of direct financing, guarantees, and backstops makes Nvidia a major player in the AI infrastructure buildout and in the world of powering data centers, especially over the past year. As energy becomes a greater strategic need for the company, it has invested in a range of power options including battery energy storage, grid software, and nuclear.

Huang’s personal involvement in forging partnerships earned him the reputation as “the bank of Huang.” This includes a slew of startups like Cloverleaf Infrastructure, Emerald AI, ThinkLabs, and Redwood Materials.

Predictably, Nvidia shares surged Monday on the news. But several power and grid companies, even those with only loose ties to the company, saw their stocks rally as well. For example, Constellation is part of a collaboration with Nvidia and other companies to develop AI factories that operate as flexible energy assets and thus can connect to the grid faster; the company’s stock increased 6%. GE Vernova is among the energy companies using Nvidia’s AI factory reference design to unlock grid capacity, and saw its stock rally by more than 8%. And even Bloom Energy, which does not have a direct Nvidia relationship but is marketing its fuel cells to match up with Nvidia’s chip roadmap, saw its stock increase by more than 18%.
As Peter Hans Hirschboeck, a founder and managing director of impactECI Energy, put it, “Market-wide, whether you are directly involved with Nvidia or not, you are affected.”

Hirschboeck added that the market response showed investors “don’t want a rudderless ship” at a company with such outsized influence on the AI industry, and indeed the entire U.S. economy, despite the scandal. “You need the guy who created the core of it to be around,” he said of current market thinking.

That said, it was just a week ago that the energy industry was adjusting to Huang’s absence. Speaking on background, one executive of an energy company with investment from Nvidia told Latitude Media last week that tech companies have been “over-dialed on the founder and CEO,” and that the over-reliance extends to the wider energy and technology ecosystem.

The spying scandal and Huang’s resignation added an additional layer of uncertainty in a moment of headwinds for the AI boom. The midterm elections gave voice to popular concerns about AI and a pushback against the boom in data center development, and investor confidence in AI companies has been waning.
articles.lede: The Nvidia CEO’s personal role in partnerships, including with energy startups, earned him the reputation as “the bank of Huang.”

articles.title: Ohio OKs gas plant for data centers despite local voter backlash
articles.description: The approval is drawing fresh criticism of Ohio’s permitting process, which has seen renewable energy projects denied or blocked due to local objections.
paragraphs: Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections.

The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition.

“ There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board.

The gas plant in question is an 800 -megawatt facility to be built at a data center complex under development in the central Ohio village of Ashville. As of now, the plant won’t be connected to the grid at large and will serve just the computing warehouses. The project site is close to homes, as well as a playground, park, and soccer field, Rader noted.

“ This plant is literally going to be throwing a shadow on these communities,” while spewing health-harming pollution, Rader said during the Power Siting Board’s Nov. 19 meeting. Yet Ohio has more stringent requirements for wind and solar, which emit zero air pollution.

Ashville’s Village Council passed a resolution in April to back the data center and gas plant project, after its developer, EdgeConneX, agreed to pay up to $ 102 million to support municipal, school, and community work. But the deal didn’t sit well with some residents, who gathered enough signatures for a referendum on whether to overturn the resolution.
On Election Day, Ashville was one of dozens of U.S. communities to reject data centers, with 81 % of the village’s voters opposing the local government’s agreement with EdgeConneX.

Even so, the Power Siting Board’s decision OK ’ing the gas plant finds that the developer met a statutory requirement that the project is in the public interest. Regulators pointed to factors like the project’s economic benefits, backing from the Village Council and local school district, and the developer’s promises to limit noise and construction hours.

That’s sparked frustration from clean energy advocates in the state. The board has denied multiple solar projects on the basis that local opposition outweighs economic benefits or has proposed permit conditions aimed at addressing community concerns, said Chris Tavenor, general counsel for the Ohio Environmental Council, which was not a party to the case.
“ In this case, the Board does the exact opposite, using those community benefits and conditions to justify ignoring local concerns,” he said in an email.
articles.lede: The approval is drawing fresh criticism of Ohio’s permitting process, which has seen renewable energy projects denied or blocked due to local objections.

articles.title: Honduras starts paying solar prosumers for excess power
articles.description: Honduras has begun compensating solar self-consumption customers for surplus electricity exported to the distribution grid, with the Zamorano University campus becoming the first eligible user under tariffs of $92.50/MWh to $111.27/MWh.
paragraphs: Empresa Nacional de Energía Eléctrica (ENEE), Honduras’s state-owned electric utility, said that Zamorano University is the country’s first self-generating electricity customer to receive financial compensation for surplus renewable power supplied to the grid. The university has a 1,954.84 kWp solar installation comprising 4,832 modules, with an authorized maximum AC output of 1,600 kW.

Located in the municipality of San Antonio de Oriente, in the department of Francisco Morazán, the system will use a bidirectional meter to record electricity drawn from the grid separately from surplus power exported to it. The exported electricity will be compensated through monthly bill credits, based on tariffs approved by the Electricity Regulatory Commission (CREE).

Honduras approved regulations that year allowing renewable self-consumption customers to receive compensation for surplus electricity exported to the grid. In 2025, the regulator expanded the rules to include commercial customers connected at medium voltage with installations larger than 1 MW, and provided for the use of energy storage systems.

Zamorano University has operated solar installations since 2015, when Enertiva completed the first phase of its solar park, with 926.4 kWp of capacity and 2,940 polycrystalline modules. In March 2021, the university inaugurated a second phase with 402 kWp of capacity, comprising 864 465 W modules installed on solar trackers.

In May 2025, the university also signed a memorandum of understanding with ENEE to develop the 14.5 MWp Energy for Education solar project, which will include lithium-ion battery storage. Revenue from electricity sales is intended to fund scholarships for Honduran students from low-income families.

articles.title: How data centers can help bring solar and batteries to homes
articles.description: Sunrun wants hyperscalers to fund residential solar and batteries, accelerating interconnections while benefiting households.
paragraphs: Sunrun thinks the homes surrounding proposed data centers could help developers address both challenges.

“Rather than spending the money you would spend to build [on-premises] or fund some new development of generation, subsidize a consumer offering for people around the data center,” Sunrun president and chief revenue officer Paul Dickson said at Latitude Media ‘s Flex Summit in Austin in October.

The idea is to use hyperscaler investment to bring solar and batteries to households in the region, creating distributed capacity that could accelerate grid connections while giving residents lower energy costs and greater resilience.

Much of the data center industry’s search for speed to power has focused on building or buying new generation. Sunrun proposes using residential resources to ease the capacity constraints holding up large-load interconnections. Those resources can be deployed incrementally, potentially faster than conventional infrastructure.

Here’s how Sunrun envisions it working: Hyperscalers would subsidize solar and battery installments in homes connected to the same grid as their developments. Sunrun would aggregate those systems into dispatchable capacity that utilities could draw on to manage grid constraints. Then, the key to accelerating large-load interconnection is convincing utilities and regulators to recognize that flexibility as a dependable planning resource.

“If we can get regulators to recognize this resource as planned capacity, you instantly lift the peak capacity headroom, can interconnect more, and have more comfort in controlling costs for consumers,” Dickson said.

At the same time, hyperscalers face a community pushback problem. A March 2026 Gallup survey found that 71% of Americans opposed construction of an AI data center in their local area. While data centers may bring regional investment and tax revenue, those benefits can feel distant to residents worried about what new electricity demand might mean for their bills.

Sunrun’s pitch to hyperscalers would offer communities tangible benefits. A resident in the same region of a proposed data center could receive a solar-plus-storage system subsidized by the company creating the new demand. The household could benefit from lower electricity bills, backup power, and reduced installation costs, while the developer could gain access to distributed capacity that helps accelerate its grid connection.

Paying for residential solar and batteries would give data center developers a practical way to address local concerns about rising electricity bills. The subsidized systems would give participating residents something more immediate and personal than regional tax revenue, while potentially helping utilities avoid or defer costly infrastructure investments.
articles.lede: Sunrun wants hyperscalers to fund residential solar and batteries, accelerating interconnections while benefiting households.

If you can’t beat ’em: VW to export 300,000 Chinese-built cars per year by 2030
articles.description: With declining sales, annual capacity cuts approaching a million units, and a wave of affordable Chinese competitors entering Western markets,...
paragraphs: With declining sales, annual capacity cuts approaching a million units, and a wave of affordable Chinese competitors entering Western markets, Volkswagen is facing down its own mortality. Rather than fighting it, the company is leaning in and announcing plans to export roughly 300,000 Made-in-China VWs per year by 2030.

American dealers won’t be getting any Made-in-China vehicles (not at first, anyway), but for Mexican, South American, Middle Eastern, African, and Southeast Asian markets, the shift to lower-cost Chinese manufacturing marks a major strategic pivot. In addition to exporting budget-friendly sedans like the Jetta VA3, Volkswagen is also considering a move to adopt Xpeng’s tech stack for up to 75% of its core European lineup.

“The sharp decline in the overall market in China remains an industry-wide challenge,” said Martin Sander, Volkswagen Group’s sales boss, before adding that VW’s “new, locally developed electric models are beginning to make an impact .”

Add in rising energy costs, continuing software issues, and serious labor disputes with the IG Metall union in Europe, and Volkswagen may not have much choice in the matter – which is why it’s not exactly surprising to see VW consider turning China into an export hub. And that 300,000 number? That may be just the start.

On Volkswagen’s third-quarter results call, CFO Arno Antlitz reportedly called that 300,000 annual export target “conservative,” adding that overseas shipments could help offset the carmaker’s weakening prospects in China.

Here’s hoping those export plans eventually expand to the US. After years of pushing upmarket, seeing a reborn electric Jetta on US lots would feel like a true return to Volkswagen’s affordable and accessible “people’s car” roots.

articles.title: Lebanon looks to ramp up solar, storage deployments
articles.description: Lebanon is working towards adding at least 3 GW of electricity generation capacity in the coming years, most of which is expected to come from solar and wind, alongside battery energy storage.
paragraphs: Lebanon’s Cabinet of Ministers has approved a plan to increase the country’s electricity generation capacity by at least 3 GW to 3.5 GW over the coming years, including a focus on deploying solar, wind and battery storage installations.
The plan was presented by the country’s Energy and Water Minister Joe Sadeh during a cabinet meeting last week.

According to a statement published by the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, Lebanese citizens currently face high energy costs and rely heavily on private generators, while national utility Électricité du Liban struggles with high operating costs and grid outages.

The newly-approved plan will see natural gas-fired power plants continue to provide baseload generation, with the government agreeing to import liquefied natural gas to supply existing power plants. It also acknowledges solar, wind and storage projects as a key way to increase generation capacity in the coming years, while committing to enhancing and rehabilitating existing hydroelectric power facilities.
The government is also exploring cooperation with Qatar to accelerate the development of new renewable energy and storage projects.
The ministerial statement says potential cooperation could involve government-to-government arrangements with private sector participation under a design-build-operate-transfer model.
Ministers also discussed investment in Lebanon’s electricity transmission network to accommodate additional generation capacity and reduce existing bottlenecks.

The government statement says work is underway to involve the private sector in distribution and collection, through distribution system operators, according to the framework adopted by the Electricity Regulatory Authority. It explains the model would split the country into geographical and technical operating zones, with performance monitored by the authority.

“This operator is responsible for reducing technical and non-technical losses and increasing collection rates, according to clear performance indicators monitored by the regulatory authority,” the statement continues. “Ownership of the network’s assets remains with the state.”
Lebanon’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 1,505 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), up from 1,081 MW at the end of 2024.
articles.lede: Lebanon is working towards adding at least 3 GW of electricity generation capacity in the coming years, most of which is expected to come from solar and wind, alongside battery energy storage.

articles.title: Wind-driven spray system cools, cleans solar panels
articles.description: Researchers have developed a water spray system that cools and cleans PV modules using a wind turbine coupled directly to a mechanical pump. In rooftop tests, the system lowered cell temperature by up to 26.7 C and increased peak power output by 18.6%.
paragraphs: A research team from Iran has designed and investigated a novel self-cooling and self-cleaning system for PV modules. The system is wind-driven, using a vertical-axis wind turbine, which drives a mechanical water pump via a belt. The pump feeds a nozzle that sprays water onto the module surface to cool it and wash away dust.

“First, the system introduces a direct mechanical conversion of wind energy into pump operation. By eliminating generators, batteries, inverters, and grid connections, the proposed system operates with zero electrical power consumption,” the team said. “This fundamental design shift eliminates parasitic pumping losses, ensuring that 100 percent of the PV-generated electrical output is preserved and utilized.”

The researchers built the vertical-axis wind turbine from two second-hand bicycle rims, a connecting rod, and a support frame. They made the blades by cutting 110 mm PVC pipes lengthwise into half-pipe sections, each 70 cm long, and sealing the ends. A belt transferred rotation from the turbine shaft to a mechanical pump, which drew water from a reservoir and sent it through a hose to a nozzle directed at the front surface of the PV module. The pump began operating at about 1 m/s and could continue running at lower speeds once started.

The team tested the system on a rooftop in Farrokhshahr, Iran, using two identical 60 W polycrystalline PV modules measuring approximately 70 cm × 70 cm each. One module received the spray, while the other served as the control. During the May-June field campaign, the researchers monitored module temperature, voltage, and current between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m. They recorded wind speed and solar irradiance every 10 minutes and logged ambient temperature and water volume hourly.

“The thermal results demonstrated that the wind-driven spray system significantly reduced the cell temperature, with a maximum temperature difference of 26.7 C between the conventional and cooled panels, corresponding to approximately 36–37% reduction during peak radiation hours,” the results said. “The daily temperature behavior indicated that the cooling effect was most pronounced during midday under high irradiance and moderate-to- high wind speeds, while in early morning and late afternoon hours, the temperature difference decreased by >76% due to lower solar radiation.”

The results show that the cooled panel generated higher output power throughout the day, with maximum power increasing from 50.1 W to 59.42 W, an 18.6% improvement. Even under low-irradiance conditions, power increased by up to 25%, indicating stable system performance. The average daily energy efficiency increased from 10.37% to 11.47%, a 10.6% improvement directly attributed to reduced thermal losses.

“Economic analysis showed that despite a <2% increase in initial and maintenance costs, key financial indicators improved substantially: net present value (NPV) increased by approximately 29%, internal rate of return (IRR) by 12.6%, and levelized cost of energy (LCOE) decreased by 11.4%, confirming the cost-effectiveness of the proposed system,” the academic group concluded. “The payback period and energy payback time decreased by approximately 10% and 9.9%, respectively.”
articles.lede: Researchers have developed a water spray system that cools and cleans PV modules using a wind turbine coupled directly to a mechanical pump.

Europe turns negative electricity prices into a flexibility signal
articles.description: Negative wholesale power prices are a useful investment signal for batteries and demand response in Europe only where subsidy design and grid bottlenecks are not distorting them, says a new Eurelectric report.
paragraphs: Negative electricity prices do not necessarily indicate a failure of European power markets. They can direct investment toward energy storage, demand-side flexibility, and electrification when they reflect actual supply and demand conditions rather than regulatory distortions or structural barriers.
This is one of the main conclusions of “ Negative prices in EU power markets ,” a new report prepared by economic consultancy Compass Lexecon for European power industry association Eurelectric.

The analysis examines negative prices across European wholesale electricity markets and distinguishes between episodes that provide economic signals for adapting the power system and those associated with contractual incentives that influence generation bids.

When negative prices reflect genuine economic conditions, they can support flexible resources. When they persist because of infrastructure constraints or poorly designed support mechanisms, they can create inefficiencies and additional costs.

The report identifies significant differences in the frequency and duration of negative prices across European electricity markets, reflecting variations in renewable penetration, storage deployment, and the technical and regulatory characteristics of each system.

Spain and the Netherlands recorded negative electricity prices during approximately 7% of the hours in 2025. Following a widespread increase between 2015 and 2024, some countries subsequently experienced stabilization or a decline, while others maintained an upward trend.

Renewable generation growth alone does not explain these differences. Demand-side flexibility, grid constraints, battery availability, and generation-related incentives also influence the frequency and severity of negative prices.

The report highlights Finland as an example of how electricity systems can adapt to economic signals. Negative prices occurred during 8.3% of the hours in 2024, falling to 5.3% in 2025. During the first half of 2026, their frequency stood at approximately 1%.
Eurelectric links this development to progress in electrification and battery energy storage, which have increased the system’s ability to absorb electricity during periods of high availability.
However, the study warns that price signals alone may not stimulate investment when regulatory barriers or infrastructure limitations remain.
articles.lede: Negative wholesale power prices are a useful investment signal for batteries and demand response in Europe only where subsidy design and grid bottlenecks are not distorting them, says a new Eurelectric report.

Jordan plans 200 MW solar, 100 MW/400 MWh storage projects
articles.description: Investor prequalification for the solar project is expected to open in February 2027, followed by prequalification for the battery storage project a month later.
paragraphs: Jordan’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources unveiled plans for new large-scale solar and storage projects during the inaugural Jordan-EU Investment Conference, held last week.
The ministry is planning to invite private investors to develop a 200 MW solar project and a 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in the new year.

Both projects will follow a build-own-operate model, with state-owned National Electric Power Company purchasing the electricity generated by the solar project and acting as the beneficiary of the storage project.
Further details, including the planned locations of the projects, are yet to be announced.

The two projects form part of a wider investment package also including plans to develop a 100 MW wind project, a 450 MW pumped-storage hydropower project, shared infrastructure for green hydrogen and green ammonia production and natural gas infrastructure projects.

According to the Jordan News Agency, the projects form part of Jordan’s efforts to attract international investment, expand private sector participation in energy infrastructure and strengthen energy security, while supporting the country’s transition towards cleaner energy sources.

Jordan’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 2,195 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the same figure reported at the end of the year prior.

In September, the country’s energy regulator approved the first 200 renewable energy systems under its revised regulatory framework, which allows consumers to access several arrangements depending on their customer category and consumption profile.

articles.title: Hydrogen shifts summer solar to winter in Japanese apartment building
articles.description: Japanese contractor Takenaka has run a hydrogen system that stores surplus summer solar power for winter use in an apartment block in central Japan for a full year and says it worked as planned, though it has published no performance data.
paragraphs: Japanese construction company Takenaka Corp. said its hydrogen-linked energy management system at a 24-unit apartment building in Kurobe, Japan’s Toyama prefecture, has moved surplus summer solar power into the winter months as intended during its first year of operation.

The system pairs I.SEM, an energy management system Takenaka developed to integrate distributed power sources such as solar arrays, batteries, and electric vehicles, with a power-to-gas hydrogen system.

Surplus solar electricity in summer is used to produce green hydrogen, which is stored in a hydrogen-absorbing alloy and converted back into electricity and heat by a fuel cell in winter, when solar output is lower. Waste heat from hydrogen storage and the fuel cell supports the building’s central hot-water supply, which runs on heat pump water heaters, according to the company’s release.

The system is installed in Building O of the fifth block of Passive Town, a housing development by YKK Real Estate in Kurobe. The seven-story building, completed in March 2025, has 2,387 m2 of floor space.

Takenaka said a one-year evaluation of the system, which started operating in April 2025, confirmed that hydrogen produced in summer was stored and later used to generate electricity in winter, and that the battery and other distributed resources were managed as planned. The company aims to supply 95% of electricity demand in the apartments themselves, excluding common areas, from on-site renewable energy alone.
The Osaka-based contractor described the project as the first installation in Japan of a hydrogen-utilizing energy management system in an apartment building.

The company did not disclose the capacity of the solar array, battery, electrolyzer, hydrogen storage, or fuel cell. Nor did it publish how much hydrogen was produced, how much electricity the fuel cell generated, or the share of demand met by on-site renewables in the first year. It said it will continue to monitor the system’s operation.

Japanese contractor Taisei Corp. has tested a similar approach for seasonal storage at a zero energy building test facility in Yokohama, using two 450 kWh lithium-ion batteries, a 5.0 Nm3/h proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer, a 2,000 Nm3 hydrogen tank, and a 5 kW fuel cell.

Other building-scale solar-to-hydrogen projects in Japan include a solar-powered hydrogen production trial at a high-rise office complex in Tokyo, whose backers also have not disclosed system capacities, and a 2023 pilot by Sekisui House-W that uses surplus rooftop solar to run a small electrolyzer in a residential building. Economic curtailment of solar has now occurred in every transmission system operator area in Japan, after reaching the Tokyo area in March 2026.

Researchers from Finland’s LUT University and Germany’s Regensburg University of Applied Sciences have identified high investment costs and the low efficiency of converting electricity to hydrogen and back as major drawbacks for seasonal hydrogen storage in residential solar systems.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia expands self-consumption rules to 50 MW
articles.description: Saudi Arabia’s updated framework sets out new connection requirements, fees and net billing rules for renewable energy systems installed for self-consumption.
paragraphs: The state-owned Saudi Electricity Regulatory Authority (SERA) has updated its rules for renewable energy generation facilities designed for self-consumption.

The regulation covers renewable power systems, including solar, wind, waste-to-energy and biofuel installations, at homes and other buildings that are designed to meet consumers’ electricity needs. It stipulates that generation and consumption must take place at the same facility and permits integrated battery storage systems.

A statement published by the Saudi Press Agency says the new rules aim to improve installation, connection and operation procedures while clarifying requirements for consumers, enhancing safety and efficiency, and protecting consumer rights.

The updated regulation raises the maximum generation system capacity covered by the framework from 2 MW to 50 MW. Grid-connected systems are now divided into four categories: 1 to 11 kW, above 11 kW to 50 kW, above 50 kW to 2 MW, and above 2 MW to 50 MW.

Systems in the first category, typically residential-scale installations, require no prior approval before installation but must be notified to the service provider and installed by an accredited contractor. There is no connection fee for this category.

Systems in the final category, above 2 MW to 50 MW, require a study permit and a generation license from SERA. The application or connection fee is set at SAR 16,500 for systems between 2 MW and 4 MW, increasing to SAR 35,000 for systems above 4 MW.

The regulation requires service providers to process connection requests in the order they are submitted via an electronic platform. Providers are also required to publish a list of qualified contractors and approved equipment, as well as details of available network capacity.
The regulation also sets out a framework for mandatory net billing, under which surplus electricity exported to the grid is credited financially.

Credits are carried forward to the next billing cycle, where they can be deducted from electricity charges. The framework says credits can be used across multiple accounts, provided the accounts belong to the same consumer, and are valid for 12 months from accrual.

SERA’s updated framework comes three years after it first issued regulations for renewable energy self-consumption. It also consolidates two existing regulatory frameworks for renewable energy self-consumption and small solar energy systems.
articles.lede: Saudi Arabia’s updated framework sets out new connection requirements, fees and net billing rules for renewable energy systems installed for self-consumption.

Want 24/7 clean power for data centers? Try giant heat batteries.
articles.description: A new report argues that clean-powered heat batteries are a cost-effective, fast, and pollution-free way for data centers to get the electricity they want.
paragraphs: Data center developers are scrambling to find enough electricity to power their energy-intensive facilities. Some are building their own fossil gas power plants. But that comes with tradeoffs — sky-high equipment costs, yearslong waits for backlogged turbines, and growing public backlash against their polluting plans.
A new report from think tank Energy Innovation proposes a faster, cheaper, and cleaner route for powering off-grid data centers: giant heat batteries that are fueled by low-cost solar and wind.

This ​ “ hybrid thermal power” approach can be cost-competitive with fossil gas in many parts of the country, said Eric Gimon, the report’s author and an Energy Innovation senior fellow. Even more important, it can deliver power within a year or two in places where renewable energy is under development, he said — much faster than the wait for a gas plant.
“ It’s a pretty simple solution that hyperscalers and developers can pursue,” Gimon said. ​ “ You can do off-grid that’s fast, clean, reliable, and affordable.”

Nevertheless, Gimon said he’s unaware of a U.S. data center taking this approach today. That’s despite the availability of heat batteries from a number of different companies, including Antora, Brenmiller Energy, Electrified Thermal Solutions, and Rondo Energy.

These energy storage systems use electricity to heat rocks, bricks, or other materials to temperatures exceeding 1, 000 degrees Celsius ( 1, 832 degrees Fahrenheit). The systems can retain that heat for hours, days, or even weeks at a time, and then dispatch it later.

Most thermal storage systems installed today supply industrial process heat for everything from food processing to cement production. But they can also use that heat to boil water, spin a steam turbine, and produce electricity.

Storing heat to make electricity has its drawbacks. The process recovers only about 40 % of the total energy that’s been put into it, mainly because of losses in converting heat to steam and then to power, Gimon said. That’s not great, compared with the typical low-to-mid- 90 % ​ “ round-trip efficiency” rate for lithium-ion batteries.
“ But when I started modeling it, I realized TES [thermal energy storage] is cost-effective,” he said.

Data centers that want to run independently of the grid and on clean energy will need to store enormous amounts of power for when solar and wind aren’t available. As long as the solar and wind power is cheap enough, and the value of the electricity being generated from the steam turbines is high enough, the efficiency losses are tolerable. In fact, thermal batteries would be cheaper than conventional lithium-ion storage over longer durations, Gimon said.
articles.lede: A new report argues that clean-powered heat batteries are a cost-effective, fast, and pollution-free way for data centers to get the electricity they want.

articles.title: US Senate passes permitting bill letting solar developers sue agencies
articles.description: The US Senate has approved a federal permitting overhaul that would shorten court challenges to energy projects and let developers of solar, wind, and other energy projects seek damages from agencies over a pattern of disparate treatment, in a Nov. 19 vote that sends the bill to the House.
paragraphs: The US Senate voted 62-33 last week to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), a bill that would overhaul how US federal agencies permit energy projects, transmission lines, and other infrastructure, and open a route for developers to sue agencies over alleged disparate treatment of their project types.

The Senate passed the bill as an amendment to H.R. 2347, a tax bill the House of Representatives had already passed, after agreeing on Nov. 18 by 69-27 to replace that bill’s text with BAAJA. The House must now act on the Senate amendment before the bill can go to the president. BAAJA was introduced in the Senate on Sept. 30 by Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), and Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), and cleared a 73-25 procedural vote on Nov. 9.

Under Section 1402 of the Senate-passed text, sponsors of 46 listed project types, including solar, onshore wind, and storage as well as fossil fuel, nuclear, and transmission projects, could sue over a permit denied in bad faith or delayed more than 60 days past a deadline as part of a pattern of disparate treatment, according to a section-by-section summary by the Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC), a Washington-based think tank. Plaintiffs would need statistical evidence comparing their treatment against the previous 10 years, and damages would range from 50% to 100% of a project’s reasonably expected construction cost.

Section 1401 would bar agencies from revoking, suspending, or materially amending a permit in effect on or after Nov. 6, 2026, subject to six exceptions, including court orders, material breaches, fraud, and urgent harm, according to BPC. Where bad-faith interference is proven, sponsors could recover 25% to 50% of development and construction costs from the federal Judgment Fund, which pays court judgments against the US government.

The bill would also cut the deadline to challenge projects under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the US law requiring environmental reviews of federal actions, from six years to 150 days, according to BPC. Courts that found a NEPA violation could only send the decision back to the agency without voiding the permit or halting the project, and the agency would have no more than 180 days to correct it, it said.

The bill’s transmission title would require the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue permits for qualifying lines, including those of 230 kV or more and projects in approved regional plans, once a state has had one year to act, according to BPC. Reconductoring, voltage upgrades, added circuits, advanced technologies, and energy storage within existing rights-of-way, the land already secured for power lines, would be exempt from NEPA and historic-preservation review.

The bill would also allow behind-the-meter resources, including batteries installed on the customer side of the utility meter, to be aggregated into wholesale electricity markets within 18 months, and would give FERC 90 days to revise its policy so data centers pay their share of grid costs plus incremental costs, said BPC.
